reference_title: Standard Practice Manual for Flexible Pavements

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Frames HMA as the material for high-performance flexible pavements, sets typical asphalt-cement content ranges by mixture type, and defines dense-graded HMA with Table 2-1 gradations as the default meaning of the term unless a specific mixture is named.
sections.body: Hot-mix asphalt (HMA) is often used for high-performance pavements. The degree of performance required is selected based on traffic conditions and the availability of materials. HMA mixtures consist of mineral aggregate and asphalt cement, proportioned to meet the design requirements for airfield pavements, roads and streets, and storage areas. In general, 4 to 6.5 percent asphalt cement content is required for asphalt base, intermediate, and surface courses, and 5 to 7 percent asphalt cement content for porous friction course (PFC) and stone matrix asphalt (SMA); however, the optimum asphalt content for a given mixture is determined by mix design procedures rather than by these general ranges. The term "hot-mix asphalt" refers to any hot asphalt mixture produced in a hot-mix plant; unless referred to directly by a specific name, it refers to dense-graded HMA with the aggregate gradations shown in Table 2-1. Much of the information in this chapter is drawn from report AATP 05-01, developed by Auburn University.
key_points: HMA is mineral aggregate plus asphalt cement, hot-mixed to meet design requirements for airfields, roads/streets, and storage areas.
Typical asphalt cement content: 4-6.5% for base/intermediate/surface courses, 5-7% for PFC and SMA; true optimum content comes from mix design, not these ranges.
Unqualified "hot-mix asphalt" means dense-graded HMA with the Table 2-1 gradations.
Much of the chapter's technical basis comes from Auburn University report AATP 05-01.
sections.applicability: Applies as general orientation whenever HMA is being selected or specified for an airfield, road/street, or storage-area pavement.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Explains why hot mixing and hot compaction give HMA its performance advantages: uniform aggregate coating, precise gradation/asphalt-content control, no curing period, rapid weather-safe construction, and post-compaction stability plus resistance to moisture and frost damage.
sections.body: The hot-mix method of preparing paving mixtures provides for thorough coating of the aggregates with a uniform film of asphalt cement and accurate control of aggregate sizes and quantity of asphalt cement. Hot-mix pavements require no curing period after being laid and are used as soon as the pavement has cooled. The paving mixture must be rolled to compact the mix while it is sufficiently hot, because rolling is ineffective after the mixture has cooled, making the mix design density unachievable. Hot-mix asphalt pavements are constructed rapidly, minimizing the probability of weather-related damage occurring immediately after construction. Immediately after adequate rolling and a cooling period, the pavement has a high degree of stability from the interlocking of the coarse and fine aggregate and adhesion of the asphalt cement, as well as a high resistance to moisture penetration and frost damage.
key_points: Hot mixing thoroughly coats aggregate and allows precise control of gradation and asphalt content.
No curing period is required; pavement is opened to traffic as soon as it cools.
Rolling must occur while the mat is still hot -- design density is unachievable once it cools.
Rapid construction limits weather-damage exposure immediately after paving.
Cooled/compacted HMA gains stability from aggregate interlock plus asphalt adhesion, with high resistance to moisture and frost damage.
sections.applicability: Explains the technical rationale for choosing HMA over alternative paving materials.

sections.title: Gradations and Layer Thickness
sections.summary: Ties Table 2-1 gradation selection to layer thickness and segregation control: minimum lift thicknesses by gradation, preferred/limiting airfield layer thicknesses, leveling-course/taper rules, and which gradation to use for surface, intermediate, and shoulder layers.
sections.body: Selection of a gradation from Table 2-1 is based on the layer thickness of the HMA to be placed and the need to limit aggregate segregation. Segregation occurs more quickly in mixes with coarser aggregates; therefore, do not use aggregate gradation No. 1 on the surface. The layer thickness for gradation No. 1 must be at least 57 mm (2.25 in), for gradation No. 2 at least 37.5 mm (1.5 in), and for gradation No. 3 at least 28.5 mm (1.1 in). Use 25-mm (1 in) thick layers of HMA only in unusual situations, such as leveling courses, since these thin layers cool quickly and are difficult to place and compact properly. The preferred thickness of the surface layer for an airfield pavement is 51 mm (2 in). Underlying layers are designed/constructed no greater than 76 mm (3 in) thick, with thickness set by the total designed thickness of the asphalt mixture; airfield surface layers are not less than 37.5 mm (1.5 in) thick. When a leveling course is applied, layers must be at least 37.5 mm (1.5 in) thick except where tapered to tie into the underlying layer (tapering is discouraged); tapered leveling-course areas must be at least 19 mm (0.75 in) thick at the thinnest part of the taper to allow minimal compaction. Before overlaying, milling the existing asphalt surface to a constant grade is preferred over placing a leveling course, since it allows each layer to be placed at constant thickness throughout. Mixes with larger maximum aggregate size tend to have lower optimum asphalt content -- potentially cheaper to produce, but more difficult to handle and compact and more prone to segregation during handling. Use gradation 2 for all airfield surface course mixtures unless the layer is thinner than 37.5 mm (1.5 in), in which case use gradation 3 (and justify any asphalt layer thickness under 37.5 mm). Use gradation 2 for intermediate layers as well, unless the layer exceeds 57 mm (2.25 in), in which case gradation 1 is allowed. Use gradation 3 for shoulders and for any layer constructed less than 37.5 mm (1.5 in) thick.
key_points: Gradation choice depends on planned layer thickness and segregation risk; never use gradation No. 1 on the surface.
Minimum lift thickness: Gradation 1 >= 57 mm (2.25 in), Gradation 2 >= 37.5 mm (1.5 in), Gradation 3 >= 28.5 mm (1.1 in); 25-mm (1 in) lifts only for unusual cases like leveling courses.
Preferred airfield surface thickness is 51 mm (2 in); underlying layers <= 76 mm (3 in); airfield surface layers not less than 37.5 mm (1.5 in).
Leveling-course/taper minimums: 37.5 mm (1.5 in) generally, 19 mm (0.75 in) at the thinnest taper point; milling before overlay is preferred to a leveling course.
Gradation 2 for airfield surface (else 3 if <37.5 mm) and for intermediate layers (else 1 if >57 mm); gradation 3 for shoulders and thin (<37.5 mm) layers.

sections.applicability: Used when selecting an HMA gradation and setting lift thickness for a specific pavement layer (surface, intermediate, base, shoulder, or leveling course).

sections.title: Uses
sections.summary: Surveys HMA course types and applications (base/intermediate/surface/PFC/SMA), the traffic/subgrade factors that drive thickness design, airfield traffic-area use, PFC/SMA restrictions, fuel-spill considerations, and requirements for new construction versus rehabilitation.
sections.body: If properly designed, HMA paving mixtures are used for an asphalt base course, intermediate course, surface course, and porous friction or stone matrix asphalt course. Wheel loads, wheel spacing, tire pressures, intensity of traffic, and subgrade strength (California Bearing Ratio, CBR) dictate the thickness of the pavement (UFC 3-260-02). For airfield pavement applications, HMA is used for intermediate and surface courses on traffic areas Type A, B, C, and D, blast areas, and any other areas (including non-traffic) where its use is economical; the four airfield traffic area types and their relation to other traffic-area nomenclature are described in UFC 3-260-02. HMA is often used on any road or street classification A through F. PFCs have been used in the past to prevent hydroplaning but have not been used in recent years on airfields, primarily due to potential raveling of the surface resulting in FOD (foreign object debris); approval from the Pavements Discipline Working Group (DWG), or its designated representative, is required before using a PFC on an airfield. Grooving is used on runways in place of PFCs to remove water from the pavement surface. SMA is used in applications requiring a rut- and abrasion-resistant surfacing, but SMA mixtures are more expensive than conventional HMA and so are not commonly used. Areas subject to fuel spills require a fuel-resistant sealer over the HMA pavement, or a fuel-resistant binder; where fuel spillage is expected, investigate the use of a rigid pavement instead. HMA is used for both new construction and rehabilitation of existing pavements. For new construction, the existing subgrade must meet the strength requirements used for design, and the subbase and base course materials must meet the design quality requirements. For rehabilitation, a condition survey of the existing pavement is needed to develop the repair design. During construction, the design for materials and thicknesses must be followed, and any construction issues must be addressed immediately, prior to placement of material, to avoid having to remove and replace the work later.
key_points: HMA courses: base, intermediate, surface, porous friction course (PFC), stone matrix asphalt (SMA).
Thickness is driven by wheel loads/spacing, tire pressure, traffic intensity, and subgrade CBR per UFC 3-260-02.

Airfield use: intermediate/surface courses on Traffic Areas A-D and blast areas; PFC needs Pavements DWG approval and is now rarely used on airfields (raveling/FOD risk); grooving is the runway alternative.
SMA gives rut/abrasion resistance but costs more, limiting its use; fuel-spill areas need a fuel-resistant sealer/binder or consideration of rigid pavement.
New construction requires subgrade/subbase/base to meet design strength and quality; rehabilitation requires a condition survey; construction issues must be corrected immediately, before placement.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting which HMA course type to specify for a given traffic area, and when scoping new-construction versus rehabilitation requirements.

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: Introduces the two equipment categories covered in this section: plant equipment that produces HMA (batch plants, drum mix plants, storage silos) and placement equipment that lays and compacts it (pavers, material transfer vehicles, joint heaters, distributors, rollers).
key_points: Plant equipment (2-2.1) covers batch plants, drum mix plants, and asphalt mixture storage silos.
Placement equipment (2-2.2) covers the asphalt spreader/paver, material transfer vehicle, joint heaters, asphalt distributor, and rollers.
sections.applicability: Container section; orients the reader to the plant-versus-placement equipment breakdown that follows.

sections.title: Plant Equipment
sections.summary: States the purpose of an asphalt plant -- proportioning and mixing aggregate and asphalt cement to a uniform mix design product -- notes both batch and drum mix plants can produce high-quality HMA (drum mix is more common in the U.S.), and stresses that mixture quality control begins at the aggregate stockpiles.
sections.body: The purpose of an asphalt plant is to produce the mixture using mix design proportions of aggregate materials and asphalt cement, and to mix the materials so that all aggregates are thoroughly coated and the mixture is uniform throughout. HMA is produced in both batch and drum mix asphalt plants; drum mix plants are common in the U.S. Either type of asphalt plant can be used to produce high quality HMA. Asphalt mixture quality control begins at the aggregate stockpiles: each aggregate stockpile must be managed to prevent segregation, mixing with adjacent stockpiles, or contamination from other materials, including underlying material.
key_points: An asphalt plant proportions aggregate and asphalt cement per the mix design and mixes them to a uniform, thoroughly coated product.
Both batch and drum mix plants can produce high-quality HMA; drum mix plants are the more common type in the U.S.
Quality control starts at the aggregate stockpiles -- prevent segregation, cross-stockpile mixing, and contamination (including from underlying material).
sections.applicability: General framing before the batch-plant, drum-mix-plant, and storage-silo subsections.

sections.title: Batch Plant
sections.summary: Describes the batch-plant components shown in Figure 2-1 (cold feed hoppers, dryer, dust collector, screening deck, hot bins, mixer, storage silo) and the calibration, operating, and quality-control practice for each, including the cold-feed calibration rate formula.
sections.body:
The components of a batch plant are illustrated in Figure 2-1: storage silo, RAP feeder, baghouse, binder storage, cold feed hoppers, cold elevator, dryer, plant scales, control house, hot elevator, silo truck scales, pug mill, and hot bins. Cold feed hoppers have individual feeders for each aggregate used in the mixture; feeders are set so that the desired percentage of each aggregate, as specified in the job mix formula (JMF), is fed into the plant, with feed rate controlled by gate opening, belt speed, or another method depending on cold-feed type. If aggregate feeders are not set as specified in the JMF: (a) one hot bin overflows while another runs low on material; (b) the produced mix gradation does not meet the design gradation; and (c) the amount of natural sand varies from the design proportion and can exceed the amount allowed by specification.

Cold Feed Bins: before a project starts, the cold feed bins are calibrated so each bin feeds its desired rate. Calibration feeds one aggregate at a time onto a belt common to all aggregates; belt speed is determined first (belt length divided by time for one revolution), then a sample of material is removed and weighed over a measured belt length (e.g., 2 m/6.5 ft). The rate of feed is R = 3600WS/L, where R = rate of feed in kg/hr (lb/hr), W = weight of sample in kg (lb), S = speed of belt in m/s (ft/s), and L = length of belt sampled in m (ft). Each aggregate is fed at four to five different feeder settings, the rate of feed determined at each, and a plot developed of feed rate versus feeder setting (gate opening, belt speed, or other setting method) for each aggregate; these plots are then used to set each cold feed bin to the desired rate.

Dryer: after the cold feed bins and feeders are set, aggregate travels up the cold elevator and through the dryer, which removes moisture down to less than 0.5% and heats the aggregate to the desired mixing/handling temperature.

Dust Collector: collects dust generated in the dryer and elsewhere in the plant and returns all or a portion of it to the mix at the hot elevator; the plant must be able to control what fraction of collected dust is returned versus removed.

Screens: aggregate exits the dryer and travels with returned dust up the hot elevator, over the screening deck, and into the hot bins. Screen sizes are chosen so oversize material is rejected and the remaining aggregate is separated into sizes, ideally proportioned so material entering each hot bin matches that bin's relative volume (example: hot bins of 3, 1.5, and 1.5 cu m/4, 2, and 2 cu yd get 50%, 25%, and 25% of material, respectively). Screens are not changed for every mix, since changing them takes effort and batch plants produce a range of mixes in a normal workday.

Hot Bins: the percentage of each hot bin used in the mixture is determined by sampling each bin and testing its gradation, then selecting bin percentages so the combined hot-bin gradation matches the JMF. Variation occurs between the combined hot-bin gradation and the gradation entering the dryer (aggregate degradation, fines lost in the dust collector), but the blended aggregate gradation actually used must match the mix design.

Mixer: after the cold feed and hot bins are set, the combined hot-bin aggregate is mixed with the approved mix design amount of asphalt binder; mixing time is roughly 5 seconds for dry mixing and 25 to 40 seconds for wet mixing, sufficient to coat all aggregate particles, producing a uniform mixture at the approved gradation, asphalt content, and temperature. The batch plant weighs the approved mix design percentages of aggregate from the hot bins and the asphalt binder, then mixes them in a pugmill.

Storage Silo: a storage silo is not required in a batch plant, but almost all asphalt plants have one or more to temporarily store material during production; a batch plant's storage silo must meet the same requirements as a drum mix plant's silo (see 2-2.1.3).
key_points: Batch-plant components (Figure 2-1): cold feed hoppers, dryer, dust collector, screening deck, hot bins, mixer/pugmill, storage silo.
Cold feed bins are calibrated per aggregate against the job mix formula; feed rate R = 3600WS/L (kg/hr, from sample weight, belt speed, sampled belt length).
Mis-set feeders cause hot-bin overflow/shortage, off-spec gradation, and natural-sand content deviating from (and potentially exceeding) spec.
The dryer removes moisture to <0.5% and heats aggregate to mixing temperature; the dust collector returns a controllable fraction of collected dust to the mix.
Screens are sized to proportion material into hot bins by relative bin volume; hot-bin percentages are set so the combined gradation matches the job mix formula.
Mixing time is about 5 sec dry / 25-40 sec wet; a storage silo is optional in a batch plant but nearly universal, and must meet drum-mix-plant silo requirements.
figures: Figure 2-1: Batch Plant (courtesy of National Asphalt Pavement Association (NAPA))
sections.applicability: Applies to producing HMA in a batch-type asphalt plant, including cold-feed calibration and hot-bin proportioning.

sections.title: Drum Mix Plant
sections.summary: Describes the drum mix plant shown in Figure 2-2, which generally runs at a higher production rate than a batch plant, controls gradation entirely at the cold feed bins (no downstream screening), and adds asphalt cement in or immediately after the drum; covers the weight-sensor cold feed bin and parallel-flow versus counter-flow dryer configurations.
sections.body:
The drum mix plant, illustrated in Figure 2-2, generally produces HMA at a higher production rate than a batch plant. Its components include a storage silo, RAP feeder, binder storage, baghouse, control house, cold feed hopper, cold elevator, dryer/mixer, and truck scales. When a drum mix plant is used, gradation is completely controlled at the cold feed bins, since no additional screening of the mixture occurs downstream. Asphalt cement is either added to the aggregate while it is inside the drum or added immediately after the aggregate passes through the drum. This plant type readily produces HMA both with and without reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP).

Cold Feed Bin: set up much like a batch plant's, but the drum mix plant additionally has a weight sensor on the aggregate feed belt that weighs the aggregate on the run, prior to the dryer. This weight must be adjusted for moisture content, since moisture is removed from the aggregate during drying; the asphalt pump adds binder based on the belt-measured aggregate weight, which yields more binder than desired unless that weight is corrected for measured moisture content.

Dryer: the burner is normally located on the high side (parallel flow) or low side (counter flow) of the drum. In a parallel-flow dryer, aggregate enters at the high end and helps shield the asphalt binder -- added inside the drum at the midpoint to two-thirds of its length -- from direct flame contact, since overheating damages the binder. A counter-flow plant has the burner at the low end, is more energy efficient than a conventional (parallel-flow) drum mixer, and produces fewer emissions; various techniques protect the binder from the flame in a counter-flow plant, including double barrels (aggregate heated in an inner drum, binder added in the outer drum), coaters (binder added to the aggregate after it exits the dryer), and heat shields.

Dust Collector: operates similarly to a batch plant's dust collector.
key_points: Drum mix plants typically out-produce batch plants and control gradation entirely at the cold feed bins (no downstream screening).
Asphalt cement is added inside the drum, or immediately after, and RAP can be incorporated readily.
The cold feed bin has a belt weight sensor; measured aggregate weight must be corrected for moisture, or the binder pump over-doses asphalt cement.

Parallel-flow dryers (burner high side) shield binder via aggregate entry point and mid-drum binder addition; counter-flow dryers (burner low side) are more energy efficient/lower-emission and use double barrels, coaters, or heat shields to protect the binder from the flame.
figures: Figure 2-2: Drum Mix Plant (courtesy of NAPA)
sections.applicability: Applies to producing HMA in a drum mix (continuous-flow) asphalt plant, including moisture correction and dryer configuration.

sections.title: Asphalt Mixture Storage Silo
sections.summary: Covers storage-silo purpose and limits: maintaining silo volume for continuous drum-plant production, the cooling/oxidation and draindown risks of over-long storage, mixture-specific storage-time limits, and the requirement to correct or disallow silo use if segregation or draindown occurs.
sections.body: Asphalt storage silos are used to store HMA mixture before it is loaded onto trucks. Storage silo volume must be maintained to support a drum mix plant's continuous flow production; silos let a plant run continuously even during a temporary shortage of trucks. Material is stored in silos for short periods of time, but if stored too long it cools excessively or oxidizes excessively, causing the asphalt binder to become hard and brittle. The asphalt binder also has the potential to drain from the aggregate during long-term storage (draindown); this is more likely with mixes having a high coarse-aggregate content, such as open-graded friction course and stone matrix asphalt, so for those mixture types storage in the silo for more than 30 minutes is not allowed. The stored mixture must still meet specification requirements when sampled and tested after storage. As a general rule, HMA dense-graded mixtures are not stored more than 3 hours in a non-insulated storage silo, or more than 8 hours in an insulated storage silo. If segregation of aggregate or draindown of asphalt binder occurs in the silo, use of the silo must be disallowed, or changes made to the equipment or process to prevent segregation and draindown.
key_points: Silo volume must support the plant's continuous-flow production and buffer against temporary truck shortages.
Over-long storage causes excessive cooling/oxidation (hard, brittle binder) and binder draindown from the aggregate.
High coarse-aggregate mixes (open-graded friction course, SMA) are limited to under 30 minutes of silo storage due to draindown risk.
General dense-graded HMA storage limits: 3 hours (non-insulated silo) or 8 hours (insulated silo); stored mix must still meet spec when tested.
If segregation or draindown occurs in the silo, disallow its use or fix the equipment/process before continuing.
sections.applicability: Applies to plants using a storage silo to buffer HMA production against truck availability, particularly for drum mix plants and draindown-prone mixture types.

sections.title: Placement Equipment
sections.summary: Introduces the five categories of HMA placement equipment covered next: the asphalt spreader/paver, the material transfer vehicle, joint heaters, the asphalt distributor, and rollers.
key_points: Placement equipment covered: asphalt spreader (paver), material transfer vehicle, joint heaters, asphalt distributor, and rollers.
sections.applicability: Container section; orients the reader to the placement-equipment subsections that follow.

sections.title: Asphalt Spreader (Paver)
sections.summary: Covers paver types (track or rubber-tired, with tamping-bar, oscillating, or vibrating screed configurations) and automatic grade control practice, including stringline/laser/GPS methods, why transverse-slope control fails for multi-lane work, and the loose-to-compacted thickness allowance.
sections.body:
Types of Spreaders: an asphalt spreader is used to place mixture types such as hot mix, cold mix, and base course material. Spreaders currently in use operate on either tracks or rubber tires and have a vibrating screed to strike off and smooth the paving mixture; some use a tamping bar in conjunction with the screed, others an oscillating screed with a vibrating compactor, and others a vibrating screed for both strike-off and initial compaction. Conventional paving machines place HMA well provided they are maintained in good mechanical condition, kept adjusted, and operated by experienced personnel; poor pavement surfaces result if the screed plates are worn or rusty, or if the tamping bars (when used) are worn or improperly adjusted.

Automatic Grade Control: asphalt spreaders must have a means of automatically controlling grade. In many cases the grade of the base course or underlying layers is controlled and the desired thickness of asphalt mixture is placed to produce the desired surface grade. When directly controlling the grade of an asphalt layer, grade control is used on both sides of the paver for the first pass; for additional passes, the existing edge is matched on one side while grade control is used on the opposite side. For roads, slope control in the paver is often used, matching the existing pavement on one side and setting the desired transverse slope on the other; controlling grade purely by transverse slope is not acceptable when multiple lanes are placed, since the resulting error increases as the number of lanes placed increases. Grade-control methods used include stringline, laser, and Global Positioning System (GPS)/automation. The asphalt mixture is placed to a desired grade with the paver, but after compaction the mix rolls down 20 to 25 percent of its loose thickness -- for example, 63.5 mm (2.5 in) of loose mix compacts to 51 mm (2.0 in) -- so the initial placement is roughly 13 mm (0.5 in) higher than the desired final compacted grade.
key_points: Pavers are track- or rubber-tire-mounted, using a vibrating screed (with tamping bar, or oscillating screed with vibrating compactor, or vibrating screed alone) for strike-off and initial compaction.
Worn/rusty screed plates or worn/misadjusted tamping bars produce a poor pavement surface, even on well-maintained machines.
Automatic grade control is required; first pass controls both sides, later passes match the existing edge on one side and control grade on the other.
Transverse-slope-only control is unacceptable for multi-lane paving, since the error compounds with each added lane; stringline, laser, and GPS/automation are the grade-control methods used.
Compaction reduces loose mat thickness by 20-25% (e.g., 63.5 mm loose to 51 mm compacted), so initial placement runs about 13 mm (0.5 in) above final grade.
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and operating an asphalt paver, including setting up grade control for single- versus multi-lane placement.

sections.title: Material Transfer Vehicle
sections.summary: Explains the material transfer vehicle's (MTV) role in reducing segregation and improving smoothness by buffering and remixing HMA between the haul truck and paver, the minimum-spec features to require, and one common internal remixing method.
sections.body: Segregation and lack of smoothness are problems that occur on many paving projects. Use of a material transfer vehicle (MTV) has been shown to minimize segregation and improve pavement smoothness. The MTV transfers HMA paving mixture from the transport truck to the hopper of the paver; it holds a substantial amount of paving mixture, allowing more freedom in mixture transport, and remixes the paving mixture to help reduce segregation that often occurs during placement. In addition to helping prevent segregation, the MTV improves pavement smoothness by allowing the paver to operate continuously (less stopping and starting) without needing to accommodate trucking operations directly; MTVs receive mixture directly into a hopper from dump trucks. Some state Departments of Transportation (DOTs) require an MTV on critical projects, such as interstate highways, so MTVs are readily available -- but not all MTVs are the same, and some work better than others at reducing segregation and improving performance. As a minimum, specify an MTV with an articulating arm that is self-propelled and operated independently from the paver, and ensure the MTV has remixing capability to minimize segregation; many machines simply transfer mix from the truck to the paver without remixing it. One remixing method uses an internal auger with blades at varying spacing -- closer together near the discharge end and farther apart near the middle of the auger where material is fed to the paver -- so the material is mixed as it is fed to the paver.
key_points: The MTV transfers HMA from the haul truck to the paver hopper, buffering transport and remixing the mix to reduce segregation.
Improves smoothness by letting the paver run continuously, independent of trucking gaps; some state DOTs require an MTV on critical projects.
Minimum spec: articulating arm, self-propelled, operates independently of the paver, with genuine remixing capability -- many transfer-only machines do not remix.
A common remixing design is an internal auger with variable blade spacing (tighter near the discharge end, wider near the mid-auger feed point).
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying equipment to control HMA segregation and improve ride smoothness on paving projects, especially critical/high-traffic corridors.

sections.title: Joint Heaters
sections.summary: Notes that spreader-mounted joint heaters warm the adjacent lane edge for a hot longitudinal joint and higher compaction, but carry an overheating risk that prohibits their use on airfields.
sections.body: Joint-heating devices attached to asphalt spreaders have been used on a number of HMA construction projects. The joint heaters heat the edge of an adjacent pavement lane during placement so a hot joint is obtained, allowing for higher compaction. Experience with joint heaters has shown a danger of overheating the existing asphalt mixture; accordingly, joint heaters are not used on airfields.
key_points: Joint heaters warm the adjacent lane's edge during placement to produce a hot longitudinal joint with higher achievable compaction.
They carry a demonstrated risk of overheating existing asphalt mixture.
Joint heaters are not permitted for use on airfields.
sections.applicability: Applies to longitudinal joint construction on roads/streets; explicitly prohibited on airfield HMA work.

sections.title: Asphalt Distributor
sections.summary: Covers distributor spray-bar setup for uniform application (nozzle cleanliness/angle/sizing, bar height, overlap), and the governing calibration references (Asphalt Institute MS-19, ASTM D2995).
sections.body: Asphalt distributors are used to apply asphalt material evenly over a pavement surface. The openings of all nozzles are cleaned of any blockages, and nozzles must be the same size and turned to the same angle relative to the spray bar to produce a uniform fan of bituminous material. The height of the spray bar above the surface being sprayed is important for uniform application: when the bar is too high or too low, a difference in application rate occurs across the spray bar, causing streaking. The spray bar height is adjusted so that a double or triple overlap of the spray fan is obtained. The Asphalt Institute's Manual Series No. 19 (MS-19) offers guidance for calibrating and checking application equipment, and ASTM D2995 details a method for determining the application rate of asphalt (bituminous) distributors. A distributor must be fully calibrated before being allowed for use on a project.
key_points: Nozzles must be unblocked, uniform in size, and set at a consistent angle to the spray bar for a uniform spray fan.
Spray-bar height above the surface controls application-rate uniformity; incorrect height causes streaking.
Bar height is set for double or triple overlap of adjacent spray fans.
Asphalt Institute MS-19 covers calibration guidance; ASTM D2995 covers the application-rate determination method.
A distributor must be fully calibrated before project use.
sections.applicability: Applies to applying tack coat, prime coat, or surface treatments with an asphalt distributor.

sections.title: Rollers
sections.summary: Surveys the three roller types used for HMA compaction (static steel-wheel, vibratory steel-wheel, rubber-tired), why combination steel/rubber rollers are barred, the compaction role and limits of each type, minimum rubber-tired-roller spec, and general rolling-operation limits.
sections.body:
A number of roller types are used for paving operations. Rollers used to compact asphalt mixtures are static steel-wheel, vibratory steel-wheel, and rubber-tired rollers. Occasionally rollers have a steel drum on one end and rubber tires on the other; these combination rollers are not allowed for use on HMA, because the rubber tires tend to pick up the asphalt mixture and damage the HMA surface.

Static Steel-Wheel Rollers: available in two-wheel (tandem) and three-wheel (tricycle) versions. Two-wheel tandem rollers are used for finish rolling but have also been used for breakdown rolling. Static steel-wheel rollers leave a smooth finish, but excessive rolling causes lateral movement of the mixture, surface cracking, and a general loss in density; these rollers must be equipped with a system for watering the drums and scrapers to remove material sticking to the drums. Three-wheel (tricycle) rollers are used less often, partly due to their tendency to push and shove the asphalt mixture, causing surface problems.

Vibratory Steel-Wheel Rollers: commonly used for breakdown and intermediate rolling. Configurations include dual-drum vibration, single-drum vibration with single-drum static, or single-drum vibration with rubber tires on the rear axle; rubber tires on a vibratory steel-wheel roller are not normally recommended, due to potential HMA pickup. These rollers are used for breakdown, intermediate, and finish rolling: breakdown rolling can be static or vibratory (though nearly all breakdown rolling now uses vibratory mode), intermediate rolling is almost always vibratory, and finish rolling is almost always static. Excessive rolling with a vibratory roller can bleed the asphalt surface, causing excessive loss of friction; the maximum number of passes in vibratory mode is limited to three. Vibratory rollers must have a watering system and drum scrapers, and do not substitute for a rubber-tired roller during intermediate rolling.

Rubber-Tire Rollers: commonly used for intermediate rolling, and also used as breakdown rollers when mixtures are excessively tender. Whether used for breakdown or intermediate rolling, rubber-tired rollers increase compaction and produce a watertight surface. For heavy-duty pavements on roads or airfields, a rubber-tired roller must have nine tires (four on one end, five on the other), a minimum total mass load of 18,180 kg (40,000 lb) or 2,020 kg (4,440 lb) per tire, and a minimum tire inflation pressure of 620 kPa (90 psi); it must have a watering system for the tires and scrapers/pads in good condition to prevent material buildup on the tires. Commercially available products applied to the tires help keep HMA from sticking; keeping the tires hot is an effective way to prevent pickup, and skirts are used in cold or windy conditions to protect the tires from excessive cooling. The rated weight of a rubber-tire roller is its loaded (ballasted) weight; an unballasted roller weighs less, so weigh it directly if actual weight is needed. Rubber-tire rollers give the best results at longitudinal cold joints and transverse transition joints between asphalt and concrete, compared with vibratory or non-vibratory steel rollers. While roller type is not specified, including a rubber-tired roller in the roller train for compaction of all heavy-duty HMA pavements is recommended.

Operation of Rollers: rollers are operated at or below 4.8 to 8 km/h (3 to 5 mph, a fast walking speed). Starts and stops must be gradual to avoid damaging the freshly laid mixture; quick turns, or any turns causing cracking of freshly laid mixture, are not allowed.
key_points: Three roller types: static steel-wheel, vibratory steel-wheel, rubber-tired; combination steel/rubber rollers are barred from HMA use (pickup damages the surface).
Static steel-wheel gives a smooth finish but excessive rolling causes lateral movement, cracking, and density loss; tricycle rollers push/shove the mix.
Vibratory steel-wheel handles breakdown (mostly vibratory now), intermediate (vibratory), and finish (static) rolling; limited to 3 vibratory passes to avoid bleeding/friction loss.

Rubber-tired rollers give the best compaction and watertight surface, plus the best longitudinal cold-joint and asphalt/concrete transition-joint results; heavy-duty spec: nine tires, >=18,180 kg (40,000 lb) total or 2,020 kg (4,440 lb)/tire, >=620 kPa (90 psi).
Rated roller weight is the ballasted (loaded) weight -- weigh the roller directly if actual weight matters.
Operate at 4.8-8 km/h (3-5 mph) with gradual starts/stops; no quick turns or turns that crack the fresh mat.
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and operating breakdown, intermediate, and finish compaction rollers for HMA placement.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Introduces the materials covered in this section: asphalt materials/binder grading (2-3.1), aggregates (2-3.2), mineral fillers (2-3.3), antistrip agents (2-3.4), and antifoam agents (2-3.5).
key_points: Materials covered: asphalt cements and other bituminous materials, aggregates, mineral fillers, antistrip agents, and antifoam agents.
sections.applicability: Container section; orients the reader to the materials subsections that follow.

sections.title: Asphalt Materials
sections.summary: Lists the bituminous materials and their governing ASTM specifications (Table 2-2), explains the two asphalt-cement grading systems (penetration vs. performance grading) and the current preference for PG grading, and states the general principle of using the softest grade consistent with traffic and climate.
sections.body: Asphalt materials used in hot-mix paving operations include the products conforming to the specifications listed in Table 2-2. Asphalt cements for use in pavement design and construction are graded or classified in one of two ways: on the basis of penetration (ASTM D946) or by the performance grading system (ASTM D6373). Currently, in the continental United States (CONUS) and many other countries, the performance grading system is used; however, in many countries, penetration grades of asphalt are obtained more easily. If performance graded asphalt is available, it is specified for any airfield project. In general, the softest grade of asphalt cement consistent with traffic and climate is used. Grade selection is based on several considerations, such as climate, traffic conditions, economics of asphalt availability, and previous regional experience; traffic conditions and economic considerations vary from project to project, but environmental conditions and regional experience are normally similar across a region. For example, in warm and hot regions, the grade of asphalt cement is primarily selected to ensure the mix is stable during summer months, while in cold regions, the grade is primarily selected to ensure the mix is not prone to cracking during winter months.
key_points: Bituminous material specifications are listed in Table 2-2 (asphalt cement, cutback types, emulsified asphalts).

Asphalt cement is graded by penetration (ASTM D946) or performance grading (ASTM D6373); PG grading is current U.S./CONUS practice, though penetration grading remains more accessible in many other countries.
Specify PG graded asphalt for airfield projects when it is available.
General principle: use the softest asphalt cement grade consistent with traffic and climate, weighing climate, traffic, economics, and regional experience.
Warm/hot-region grading targets summer stability; cold-region grading targets winter cracking resistance.
tables: Table 2-2: Specification References for Asphalt Materials
sections.applicability: Applies as the entry point for selecting an asphalt binder specification and grading system for any HMA project.

sections.title: Performance Graded (PG) Asphalt Cements
sections.summary: Explains that the PG system (ASTM D6373) classifies binders by performance properties tied to expected high/low pavement service temperatures, cites AASHTO R29 for grading/verification, and notes PG grading now covers both unmodified and polymer-modified binders, replacing penetration/viscosity grading in the U.S.
sections.body: The performance grading system (ASTM D6373) classifies asphalt binders using performance-related properties according to the upper and lower temperatures expected during the life of the pavement. American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) R29 provides guidance for grading or verifying the performance grade of asphalt cement. PG asphalts have replaced penetration- and viscosity-graded asphalts in the United States. Unlike the viscosity and penetration grading systems, the performance grading system is used to classify unmodified as well as polymer-modified asphalt binders.
key_points: PG grading (ASTM D6373) is keyed to expected high and low in-service pavement temperatures.
AASHTO R29 provides the grading/verification procedure for performance-graded asphalt cement.
PG grading has replaced penetration and viscosity grading in the U.S.
PG grading classifies both unmodified and polymer-modified binders, unlike the older systems.
sections.applicability: Applies when interpreting or specifying a performance-graded (PG XX-YY) asphalt cement.

sections.title: Classification Method for PG Graded Asphalt Cements
sections.summary: Covers PG base-grade selection practice (match the local state DOT base grade, low-temperature grade floor of PG XX-22), rutting-driven grade bumping for slow-traffic/stacking areas and tire pressure, the PG-grade-sum rule of thumb for polymer modification, and polymer-modification effects/verification (elastic recovery, forced ductility, phase angle, the emerging MSCR test).
sections.body:
Specify PG graded asphalt binders wherever available. The same PG binder grade used by the state highway department in the specific geographic area is considered as the base grade for the project (e.g., the PG grade specified in that location for dense-graded mixes on highways with design equivalent single axle loads (ESAL) less than 10 million). The exception is that grades with low temperature requirements higher (less negative) than PG XX-22 (e.g., PG XX-16 or PG XX-10) are not used, unless the engineer or the local DOT has had successful experience with those grades.

Rutting is not typically a problem on airfield runways but has occurred on taxiways, where traffic moves more slowly, and at airfields with a history of aircraft stacking at the ends of runways and on taxiways. Where rutting has occurred on a project, or stacking occurs regularly during the design life, grade "bumping" is applied to the top 125 mm (5 in) of paving in runway-end and taxiway areas: for aircraft tire pressure between 0.7 and 1.4 MPa (100-200 psi), the high-temperature grade is increased by one grade; for tire pressure greater than 1.4 MPa (200 psi), by two grades. For projects supporting air operations on ships, a two-grade high-temperature increase is required for all HMA projects.

PG grades are provided in 6-degree Celsius increments (e.g., PG 64-22, PG 70-22, PG 76-22 on the high-temperature side; PG 64-22, PG 64-28 on the low-temperature side). Many state DOTs in southern climates have selected a mid-range high-side grade, PG 67-22, as their primary binder grade; in those states, PG 67-22 is specified unless the high-temperature grade needs bumping for rutting resistance. Polymer-modified asphalt (PMA) improves rutting resistance and results in a bumped grade of asphalt binder; when bumping the high-temperature grade, the low-temperature grade is kept the same as that of the base grade asphalt. A rule of thumb: an asphalt binder whose high- and low-temperature grade numbers sum to more than 90 is likely to contain a polymer -- e.g., PG 64-22 sums to 86 (likely not modified), while PG 76-22 sums to 98 (almost certainly modified). Bumping from PG 64-22 to PG 76-22 provides much improved rutting resistance but substantially increases mixture cost (on the order of 15%, though this varies considerably).

Polymer Modification of Asphalts: many polymers improve the stiffness and flow characteristics of asphalt at high temperatures and have been shown to significantly reduce rutting where it has been a problem; polymer-modified mixtures are produced at higher mixing temperatures to facilitate mixing, placement, and compaction. Polymers also improve low-temperature characteristics, improving resistance to low-temperature cracking. Many agencies bump the binder grade both to improve rutting resistance and to help ensure the binder contains a polymer (for example, bumping a PG 64-22 to a PG 76-22 increases high-temperature stiffness without increasing low-temperature stiffness, producing a more rut-resistant mixture without increasing cracking potential). However, the grade can also be bumped by other means, such as air blowing, without the improved performance a true polymer provides. Ensuring a polymer is used to bump the grade requires modifying the binder specification -- modifications used include elastic recovery, forced ductility, and phase angle requirements -- and differing agency requirements for this have created problems for asphalt binder producers, prompting development of the multiple stress creep recovery (MSCR) test. The MSCR test is still being finalized and is not yet part of the standard specifications; when the PG binder grade is bumped, adopting additional PG binder requirements ("PG plus") specified by the local state DOT is recommended, until the MSCR test procedure is completed and adopted into the ASTM binder specifications.
key_points: Base PG grade should match the local state DOT's grade for that geography (e.g., dense-graded highway mixes with ESAL < 10 million); low-temperature grades warmer than PG XX-22 need engineer/DOT experience to justify.

Rutting-prone slow-traffic/stacking areas get high-temperature grade bumping to the top 125 mm (5 in): +1 grade at 0.7-1.4 MPa (100-200 psi) tire pressure, +2 grades above 1.4 MPa (200 psi); ship-support airfields require +2 grades on all HMA.
PG grades step in 6degC increments; many southern-climate DOTs use PG 67-22 as the primary high-side grade.
Rule of thumb: PG grade-number sum > 90 indicates polymer modification (PG 64-22 = 86, unmodified; PG 76-22 = 98, modified); bumping raises cost roughly 15% (varies).
When bumping for rutting resistance, keep the low-temperature grade unchanged from the base grade.
Polymer modification improves both high-temperature rutting resistance and low-temperature cracking resistance, but requires higher mixing temperatures.

Grade bumping alone does not guarantee polymer use (e.g., air blowing can bump grade without polymer performance); verification relies on elastic recovery/forced ductility/phase-angle spec add-ons or local "PG plus" requirements pending the still-unfinalized MSCR test.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting or specifying a PG asphalt binder grade, including rutting-driven grade bumping and verifying polymer modification.

sections.title: Asphalt Cement Selection by Temperature Region
sections.summary: Gives the full climate-based binder selection procedure: computing the Pavement Temperature Index (PTI) to assign a Cold/Warm/Hot region and base grade from Table 2-3 (worked example, Table 2-4), determining the Design Air-Freezing Index (DFI) for cold regions to set the low-temperature grade from Table 2-5 and Figure 2-3, and three fully worked region examples.
sections.body:
Determining the Temperature Region: Table 2-3 gives guidance for selecting penetration-graded and performance graded asphalt binder by temperature region. When local experience (e.g., a state DOT's own requirements) indicates a specific asphalt binder grade, that local experience controls. Absent local experience, climatological data is used: average monthly maximum temperature data is first used to compute a pavement temperature index (PTI). When project-location average monthly maximum temperatures are above 23.9 degC (75 degF), the PTI is the sum of the monthly increments exceeding 23.9 degC (75 degF); conversely, when no average monthly maximum exceeds 23.9 degC (75 degF), the PTI is the difference between the highest average maximum temperature (warmest month) and 23.9 degC (75 degF). Table 2-3 bands: PTI < 16.7 degC (30 degF) is a Cold region, using 120-150 penetration or PG (52,58)-xx (see paragraph 2-3.1.3.3, as cross-referenced in the source, for cold-region low-temperature grade guidance); 16.7-44.4 degC (30-80 degF) is a Warm region, using 85-100 penetration or PG 64-(22 or 28); and greater than 44.4 degC (80 degF) is a Hot region, using 60-70 penetration or PG (64, 70, or 76)-22. Table 2-3 is used only absent local guidance on asphalt cement grade.

Example of Calculations for PTI: for two example construction sites (Table 2-4), the average monthly maximum temperature and the difference above 23.9 degC (75 degF) are tabulated month by month; the cumulative PTI is the sum of the monthly increments above 23.9 degC (75 degF). Site A totals 54.2 cumulative degC (97.6 cumulative degF), classifying it a Hot region; Site B totals 1.1 cumulative degC (2.0 cumulative degF), classifying it a Cold region, per the Table 2-3 bands.

Cold Region Requirements -- Determining the Design Air-Freezing Index: when a project falls in a cold region per Table 2-3, additional climate data is needed -- a design air-freezing index (DFI), determined per UFC 3-260-02 -- to meet cold-region requirements. DFIs differentiate between climates within cold temperature regions: a DFI of 1,667 degree Celsius-days (3,000 degree Fahrenheit-days) is the delineation between moderately cold and severely (extremely) cold climates. Moderately cold climates have DFIs up to 1,667 degree-days; severely cold climates have DFIs greater than 1,667 degree-days. After determining DFI, the asphalt grade is selected from Table 2-5. The minimum anticipated pavement temperature is estimated as a function of DFI in Figure 2-3; knowing this minimum pavement temperature helps select the best low-temperature binder grade -- the selected low-temperature grade must be lower (colder) than the Figure 2-3 estimate (e.g., an estimated low pavement temperature of -26 degC (-14.8 degF) calls for a PG grade of -28 or lower).

Examples of Asphalt Cement Selection in the Three Regions:
(a) Hot region: a parking lot in a region with PTI 54.4 cumulative degC (97.6 cumulative degF). If the DOT requires PG 67-22 for routine traffic and PG 76-22 for heavy traffic (e.g., an Interstate Highway), select PG 67-22 generally, or PG 76-22 in areas of known potential rutting (slow-moving airfield traffic areas including taxiways and runway ends, and roads with high-volume and/or slow-moving traffic). Absent local guidance, Table 2-3 gives 60-70 penetration or PG (64, 70, 76)-22; PG 76-22 is preferred where rutting has been a problem or aircraft stacking is expected, PG 64-22 is selected for shoulders or low-traffic areas, and PG 70-22 works reasonably well in traffic or non-traffic areas.
(b) Warm region: a street in a region with PTI 23.3 cumulative degC (42 cumulative degF). Per Table 2-3, 85-100 penetration asphalt cement or PG 64-(22, 28) is selected absent local guidance; the -28 low-temperature grade is more resistant to cracking, the -22 more economical.
(c) Cold region: a heavy-duty open storage area (design index of 0) for 22,680-kg (50,000-lb) forklift trucks, in a region with PTI 1.1 cumulative degC (2 cumulative degF) and a DFI of 1,278 degree Celsius-days (2,300 degree Fahrenheit-days) calculated per UFC 3-260-02. Penetration 120-150 is used if penetration-graded asphalt is used, or PG (52, 58)-(28, 34) based on Tables 2-3 and 2-5; Grade 58 is more rut resistant and Grade -34 is more crack resistant.
key_points: PTI = sum of monthly average-maximum-temperature increments above 23.9 degC (75 degF); or, if none exceed that threshold, the (negative) difference of the warmest month's average maximum below it.

Table 2-3 bands by PTI: Cold (<16.7 degC/30 degF) -> 120-150 pen or PG(52,58)-xx; Warm (16.7-44.4 degC/30-80 degF) -> 85-100 pen or PG64-(22,28); Hot (>44.4 degC/80 degF) -> 60-70 pen or PG(64,70,76)-22; use only absent local DOT guidance.
Worked PTI example (Table 2-4): Site A = 54.2 degC (97.6 degF) cumulative -> Hot; Site B = 1.1 degC (2.0 degF) cumulative -> Cold.

Cold-region projects additionally need a Design Air-Freezing Index (DFI, per UFC 3-260-02); 1,667 degC-days (3,000 degF-days) splits moderately from severely cold and sets the Table 2-5 grade and Figure 2-3 minimum pavement temperature.

Three fully worked examples cover hot (parking lot, PG 67-22 vs. 76-22 by rutting exposure), warm (street, PG 64-22 vs. -28), and cold (forklift storage yard, DFI-driven PG 52/58-28/34) region binder selection.
