sections.title: Aggregates
sections.summary: Sets the general aggregate quality principle -- clean, hard, durable, and angular -- and the crushing/fines-removal practice used to convert rounded natural sand/gravel sources into angular, fractured aggregate suitable for stable HMA.
sections.body: Clean, hard, and durable aggregates are used for HMA. Angular aggregates provide more stable HMA mixtures than rounded aggregates; natural sands and gravels tend to be rounded and must be limited, or the gravel crushed, to provide angular properties. Fine aggregate is removed from the source stone material before crushing to remove soft particles and potential clay balls that develop in the seams of the rock. Fine aggregate is likewise removed from the gravel source before crushing, to remove potential soft particles and clay balls and to ensure that, after crushing, particles are fractured and angular.
key_points: Aggregate must be clean, hard, and durable; angular aggregate gives more stable HMA than rounded aggregate.
Natural sand/gravel is rounded and must be limited, or the gravel crushed, to achieve angularity.
Fines are removed from stone and gravel sources before crushing, to eliminate soft particles/clay balls and ensure crushed particles come out fractured and angular.
sections.applicability: General framing before the individual aggregate test-method subsections that follow.

sections.title: Sieve Analysis
sections.summary: Covers the sieve analysis procedure (ASTM C136) that an experienced engineer uses to judge aggregate suitability, asphalt content needs, and filler needs, and the distinction between dry (QC) and washed (acceptance) gradations.
sections.body: Aggregates used in a paving mix, as listed in Table 2-1, are subjected to a sieve analysis. From an aggregate's grading curve, an experienced engineer obtains information concerning the suitability of the aggregate for a paving mix, the quantity of asphalt cement required, and whether mineral filler needs to be added. Sieve analyses of fine and coarse aggregates are conducted according to ASTM C136. Washed sieve analysis is needed to get an accurate measure of dust (minus No. 200 material), but for quality control (QC) testing during construction, dry gradations are conducted to reduce test time; washed gradations are used for acceptance testing.
key_points: Sieve analysis (ASTM C136) informs aggregate suitability, required asphalt content, and filler needs from the grading curve.
Washed sieve analysis is needed for an accurate dust (minus No. 200) measurement.
Dry gradations are used for construction QC testing (faster); washed gradations are used for acceptance testing.
sections.applicability: Applies to routine gradation testing of aggregate stockpiles and produced mixture.

sections.title: Specific Gravity
sections.summary: States that bulk specific gravity of coarse and fine aggregate (ASTM C127/C128) is required input for computing percent VMA.
sections.body: Bulk specific gravity values for aggregates used in a paving mixture are required for the computation of percent VMA. The method for determining bulk specific gravity of aggregate is provided in ASTM C127 for coarse aggregate and ASTM C128 for fine aggregate.
key_points: Bulk specific gravity of aggregate is a required input to the percent VMA computation.
Coarse aggregate bulk specific gravity: ASTM C127. Fine aggregate bulk specific gravity: ASTM C128.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever VMA must be computed for mix design or QC/acceptance testing.

sections.title: Abrasion and Impact Resistance of Coarse Aggregate
sections.summary: Covers the Los Angeles Abrasion test (ASTM C131) for coarse-aggregate degradation resistance, and when it can be waived based on prior performance.
sections.body: Determination of percent loss for coarse aggregates is not required if the aggregate has been found to meet the project mix design by previous tests or performance; however, coarse aggregates obtained from new or doubtful deposits are tested for resistance to degradation by evaluating conformance to specification requirements for percent loss, as measured using the Los Angeles Abrasion Machine (ASTM C131).
key_points: Percent-loss (LA Abrasion, ASTM C131) testing can be waived for aggregate with a proven mix design/performance history.
New or doubtful-source coarse aggregate must be tested against the specification's percent-loss limit.
sections.applicability: Applies to qualifying coarse aggregate sources for degradation resistance, particularly new or unproven sources.

sections.title: Soundness Test
sections.summary: Covers the sodium/magnesium sulfate soundness test (ASTM C88) used to check freeze-damage resistance, and when it can be waived based on prior performance.
sections.body: The soundness test is used where damage from freezing is a potential problem. The soundness test is not performed on aggregate that has been found to meet the mix design by previous tests or performance data; however, aggregate obtained from new or doubtful deposits is tested for conformance to specification requirements using the sodium sulfate or magnesium sulfate solution tests (ASTM C88).
key_points: Soundness testing addresses freeze-damage susceptibility of aggregate.
Waived for aggregate with a proven mix design/performance history; required (ASTM C88, sodium or magnesium sulfate) for new or doubtful-source aggregate.
sections.applicability: Applies in freeze-susceptible climates when qualifying new or unproven aggregate sources.

sections.title: Percent Crushed Pieces
sections.summary: Covers the CRD-C 171 crushed-particle-percentage requirement for coarse aggregate, the contract-spec need to define a crushed face, and why natural gravels versus crushed stone differ in how easily they meet the requirement.
sections.body: The percentage of crushed pieces in both the coarse aggregate and fine aggregate fractions must be sufficiently high to promote stability in the HMA mix design. CRD-C 171 is used to determine the percentage of crushed aggregate particles for coarse aggregate (particles retained on a 4.75 mm (No. 4) sieve). A description of a crushed face and the required percentage of crushed aggregate particles must be specified in the contract specifications. Natural gravels require crushing to produce the mix design percentage of fractured faces; crushed stone, on the other hand, almost always meets the fractured-face requirement.
key_points: Crushed-particle percentage in coarse and fine fractions must be high enough to promote HMA stability.
CRD-C 171 determines percent crushed particles for coarse aggregate retained on the 4.75 mm (No. 4) sieve.
Contract specs must define a crushed face and the required crushed-particle percentage.
Natural gravels need crushing to meet the fractured-face requirement; crushed stone almost always meets it inherently.
sections.applicability: Applies when qualifying gravel or stone aggregate sources for angularity/crushed-face requirements.

sections.title: Particle Shape
sections.summary: Covers the cubical-particle-shape requirement for crushed aggregate and the flat-and-elongated-particle test (ASTM D4791) used to check conformance.
sections.body: The particle shape of crushed aggregates is required to be essentially cubical. Flat and elongated aggregate particles are susceptible to breakage under compaction and subsequent traffic; this breakdown of aggregate results in a change in the volumetric properties of the mixture, often resulting in a mix that does not meet specification requirements. The quantity of flat and elongated particles is determined for conformance to specification requirements using ASTM D4791.
key_points: Crushed aggregate particle shape must be essentially cubical.
Flat/elongated particles break down under compaction and traffic, shifting mixture volumetric properties out of spec.
Flat-and-elongated-particle content is measured per ASTM D4791.
sections.applicability: Applies when qualifying crushed aggregate for particle-shape conformance.

sections.title: Clay Lumps and Friable Particles
sections.summary: Covers the clay-lumps-and-friable-particles test (ASTM C142), which screens out aggregate containing clay balls or soft particles that break down under handling/traffic and cause FOD-relevant blemishes.
sections.body: Some aggregates tend to have clay balls and soft particles. This test requirement (ASTM C142) evaluates the aggregate to ensure that aggregate containing clay balls or other friable particles, which tend to break down during handling or traffic, is not allowed in the asphalt mixture. While these particles do not normally cause disintegration of the pavement, they do result in blemishes that are unsightly and lead to FOD, which is a significant problem for airfield pavements.
key_points: ASTM C142 screens out aggregate containing clay balls or friable (soft, breakdown-prone) particles.
These particles rarely disintegrate the pavement itself but cause unsightly blemishes and generate FOD -- a significant airfield-pavement concern.
sections.applicability: Applies particularly to airfield HMA, where FOD risk from friable particles is a significant operational concern.

sections.title: Sand Equivalent
sections.summary: Covers the sand equivalent test (ASTM D2419), which measures the sand-to-clay-size particle ratio in fine aggregate and disqualifies fine aggregate that fails.
sections.body: Some aggregates contain a significant amount of clay particles distributed throughout the aggregate. These particles, which are not identified by the clay lumps and friable particles test, present a problem. The sand equivalent test (ASTM D2419) evaluates a fine aggregate to determine the ratio between sand-size and clay-size particles. When a fine aggregate fails the sand equivalent test, it is not acceptable for use.
key_points: Sand equivalent (ASTM D2419) catches distributed clay content that the clay-lumps/friable-particles test misses.
Measures the ratio between sand-size and clay-size particles in fine aggregate.
Fine aggregate failing the sand equivalent test is unacceptable for use.
sections.applicability: Applies to qualifying fine aggregate for distributed (non-lump) clay content.

sections.title: Natural Sand Content
sections.summary: Covers the 15% natural (uncrushed) sand limit for airfield mixtures, why excess natural sand destabilizes HMA and weakens asphalt bond, and the requirement to account for natural sand carried in RAP.
sections.body: Natural sand is defined as any fine aggregate material that occurs naturally and has not been crushed. Natural sands tend to be rounded particles which, when used in excess, cause instability in the HMA mixture. The limit of 15 percent natural (uncrushed) sand in airfield mixtures assures a strong and stable pavement under aircraft. Natural sand also tends to have a smooth surface, often resulting in a poor bond between the asphalt binder and the sand particles. When reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP) is used, the amount of natural sand in the RAP is determined and included in the total amount of natural sand in the recycled mixture.
key_points: Natural (uncrushed) sand is rounded and destabilizes HMA when used in excess.
Airfield mixtures are limited to 15 percent natural sand to assure a strong, stable pavement under aircraft loading.
Natural sand's smooth surface often produces a poor asphalt-binder bond.
Natural sand carried in RAP must be quantified and counted toward the total natural sand content of the recycled mixture.
sections.applicability: Applies to fine-aggregate blend proportioning for airfield HMA mixtures, including RAP mixes.

sections.title: Fine Aggregate Angularity
sections.summary: Covers the FAA test (ASTM C1252 Method A), typical FAA values for crushed versus natural fine aggregate, and the default minimum specified FAA of 45.
sections.body: The fine aggregate angularity (FAA) test method (ASTM C1252, Method A) measures the uncompacted void content in the fine aggregate portion of a mix and is related to the angularity of the fine aggregate portion of the mixture. Generally, crushed fine aggregates have an FAA value greater than 45, while natural sands have FAA values between the high 30s and the low 40s. The minimum specified value of FAA is 45, unless local experience indicates that aggregates with a lower value provide better performance. Occasionally, the FAA of a fine aggregate portion of the total aggregate is less than 45 even when it contains 100 percent crushed stone particles.
key_points: FAA (ASTM C1252, Method A) measures uncompacted void content of fine aggregate, correlating with angularity.
Typical values: crushed fine aggregate > 45 FAA; natural sand high-30s to low-40s FAA.
Default minimum specified FAA is 45, unless local experience supports a lower value.
A fine aggregate fraction can occasionally test below 45 FAA even at 100 percent crushed-stone content.
sections.applicability: Applies to qualifying fine aggregate angularity for HMA mix design and acceptance.

sections.title: Voids in Mineral Aggregate (VMA)
sections.summary: Defines VMA as the intergranular void volume in compacted aggregate (a packing-ability measure, not an aggregate property per se), lists its governing inputs, and explains why the VMA requirement indirectly sets the minimum asphalt content in a mix design.
sections.body: The VMA is the volume of intergranular void space between the aggregate particles of a compacted paving mixture, expressed as a percent of the total volume; it includes the air voids and the volume of asphalt not absorbed into the aggregates. While VMA is not an aggregate property, it is a measure of the packing ability of an aggregate. The VMA is a function of the bulk specific gravity of the aggregate, the bulk specific gravity of the mix, the asphalt content, and the specific gravity of the asphalt binder. The VMA requirement is used to establish the minimum amount of asphalt binder added to the asphalt mix design; without the VMA requirement, laboratories would design asphalt mixes with less asphalt binder to reduce mix cost. These low-asphalt-content mixes are difficult to place and compact and often result in reduced pavement durability. The VMA requirement indirectly controls the minimum asphalt content.
key_points: VMA = intergranular void volume (air voids plus unabsorbed asphalt) in compacted paving mixture, as a percent of total volume.
VMA is not an aggregate property itself, but a measure of packing ability, driven by aggregate/mix bulk specific gravity, asphalt content, and asphalt specific gravity.

The VMA requirement indirectly sets the minimum asphalt content in the mix design -- without it, mixes would be designed with too little asphalt to save cost, hurting placement/compaction and durability.
sections.applicability: Applies to HMA mix design volumetric criteria and to setting/checking minimum asphalt content indirectly through VMA.

sections.title: Combining Aggregates
sections.summary: Notes that asphalt mixtures typically blend aggregate from multiple sources and describes the engineering-judgment options (regrade, substitute, or adjust the mix) when a blend fails to meet criteria.
sections.body: When asphalt mixtures are produced, aggregates from two or more sources are combined. This UFC provides methods and procedures for determining the aggregate blend available and prescribing the asphalt content for the aggregate blend. Whenever an asphalt mixture does not meet established criteria, the gradation of the aggregate is improved, another aggregate is used, or adjustments are made in the mix. The choice among these options is a matter of engineering judgment by the contractor, involving an analysis of the available aggregate supplies and costs.
key_points: Asphalt mixtures typically combine aggregate from two or more sources.
This UFC provides procedures for determining the available aggregate blend and prescribing its asphalt content.
When a blend fails to meet criteria, options are improving the gradation, substituting another aggregate, or adjusting the mix -- an engineering-judgment call weighing available supply and cost.
sections.applicability: Applies when a single aggregate source cannot meet the specified gradation/blend requirements on its own.

sections.title: Mineral Fillers
sections.summary: Defines mineral filler as material passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve, notes that most mixtures already carry enough filler in the aggregate (and some carry too much), and requires commercial fillers to conform to ASTM D242.
sections.body: Mineral filler refers to the material passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve. Most asphalt mixtures have enough mineral filler in the crushed aggregates and no additional filler is required. In fact, many mixtures have too much filler in the aggregates, and procedures have to be used to waste some of the filler prior to or during plant production operations. Some mineral fillers are more desirable to use in asphalt paving mixtures than others; for example, fine sands are less suitable fillers than limestone filler or some other by-product of crushed stone. Asphalt pavement mixtures are designed using commercial fillers that conform to ASTM D242.
key_points: Mineral filler is material passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve.
Most mixtures already carry sufficient filler in the crushed aggregate; some carry too much and must waste excess filler before/during production.
Fine sands make a less suitable filler than limestone filler or other crushed-stone byproducts.
Commercial fillers used in mix design must conform to ASTM D242.
sections.applicability: General framing before the mineral-filler-addition subsection that follows.

sections.title: Addition of Mineral Filler
sections.summary: Explains when and how much mineral filler to add, and the competing effects of too-low versus too-high filler content on VMA, asphalt content, stability, and durability, giving practical target filler percentages.
sections.body: Additional filler is seldom needed in asphalt mixtures, since the aggregates typically contain sufficient filler. The quantity of mineral filler to be added or removed depends on the amount of filler naturally present in the aggregate; in most cases the amount of filler in the aggregate produces a mixture meeting the specification requirements. With some aggregates, washing is performed to remove excess filler in the aggregate before producing an asphalt mixture. High filler contents reduce the VMA in the mixture, making it difficult to meet specification requirements for VMA. The addition of satisfactory mineral filler, when needed, results in lower optimum asphalt content and increased stability of a paving mixture. Mixtures with low filler contents typically require additional asphalt binder to fill the voids, resulting in a mixture that tends to be less stable if the filler is too low. Higher amounts of filler result in lower optimum asphalt content and reduced film thickness, causing a loss in mixture durability. Practical considerations and optimum performance usually dictate quantities of approximately 5-6 percent passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve for HMA, and approximately 10 percent passing for sand-asphalt mixtures.
key_points: Added filler is seldom needed; the quantity added or removed depends on the amount already naturally present in the aggregate.
Excess filler is sometimes removed by washing the aggregate; high filler content reduces VMA below spec.
Adequate added filler lowers optimum asphalt content and increases stability; too little filler forces more asphalt to fill voids and reduces stability.
Too much filler lowers optimum asphalt content and film thickness, reducing durability.
Practical target: ~5-6% passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve for HMA, ~10% for sand-asphalt mixtures.
sections.applicability: Applies to mix design decisions on whether and how much mineral filler to add.

sections.title: Antistrip Agents
sections.summary: Surveys antistrip agent categories and dosing points (refinery-added liquid antistrip vs. plant-added hydrated lime and other agents), and cites the tensile strength ratio test (ASTM D4867/D4867M) used to evaluate stripping resistance.
sections.body: Several antistrip agents have been used successfully to reduce the probability of asphalt stripping from the aggregate. Antistrip agents are added to the asphalt binder before it leaves the refinery, while others are added directly into the mixer as mineral filler. Hydrated lime is a commonly used antistrip agent, with a history of success in preventing stripping. Liquid antistrip agents are easier to work with, since they are mixed into the asphalt at the refinery and do not require any extra effort by the contractor; when hydrated lime is added at the plant, a silo to hold the lime and equipment to meter it into the mix are required, meaning more effort by the contractor. Other available antistripping agents fall into these general groups: cationic surfactants, iron naphthenate, organosilane, and Portland cement. The tensile strength ratio (TSR) (ASTM D4867/D4867M) is used to evaluate the stripping property of a dense-graded asphalt mixture.
key_points: Antistrip agents are added either at the refinery (liquid, mixed into the binder) or at the plant mixer (e.g., hydrated lime as filler).
Hydrated lime has the strongest track record of preventing stripping; liquid refinery-added agents require less contractor effort than plant-metered lime.
Other antistrip agent categories: cationic surfactants, iron naphthenate, organosilane, Portland cement.
Tensile strength ratio (TSR, ASTM D4867/D4867M) evaluates stripping resistance of dense-graded HMA.
sections.applicability: General framing before the recommended-antistrip-agent subsection that follows.

sections.title: Recommended Antistrip Agent
sections.summary: Recommends 1 percent hydrated lime by weight as the antistrip agent, notes dosage is set by trial-and-error testing, and flags the practical cost/logistics difference between "lime states" and non-lime states.
sections.body: The recommended procedure for improving the resistance of an aggregate to stripping is to add 1 percent by weight hydrated lime to the mixture; this 1 percent lime is included in the determination of the aggregate gradation. Exact amounts are determined through trial and error on test specimens with various amounts of antistripping materials. Research has shown that lime provides better resistance to stripping than other materials. Some state DOTs are considered lime states and others are not; when working in a state that does not use lime, local contractors are typically not set up to add lime, increasing the cost of setting up equipment to store and feed lime into the mix.
key_points: Recommended dosage is 1 percent hydrated lime by weight, counted in the aggregate gradation determination.
Exact dosage is set by trial-and-error testing of specimens across a range of antistrip material amounts.
Research indicates lime outperforms other antistrip materials.
In non-"lime states," local contractors often lack lime storage/feed equipment, raising project setup cost.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and dosing an antistrip agent, and when budgeting for lime storage/feed equipment in non-lime-state markets.

sections.title: Antifoam Agents
sections.summary: Covers silicone antifoam additives used to suppress moisture-driven foaming in asphalt binder, their typical dosage, and their secondary benefits for silo hardening and truck slumping.
sections.body: Silicone additives or modifiers reduce foaming of asphalt mixes when they come in contact with moisture. Silicone additives have been used successfully to suppress foaming of asphalt in asphalt plants. The silicone used for this purpose is mixed at a rate of 1 milliliter per 640 liters (1 ounce per 5,000 gallons) of asphalt binder; the recommended range is also given as 1 to 2 parts per million. Silicones have been used to reduce the hardening of HMA while it is in storage silos, and silicone additives have successfully prevented slumping of mixes in trucks, which occurs when the hot-mix gradation is such that the mix traps escaping steam. In addition, silicones have provided better finishing qualities to pavement mixtures.
key_points: Silicone antifoam additives suppress moisture-driven foaming of asphalt binder in asphalt plants.
Typical dosage: about 1 mL per 640 L (1 oz per 5,000 gal) of binder, also expressed as 1-2 parts per million.
Secondary benefits: reduced HMA hardening during silo storage and prevention of truck slumping (steam-trapping) in gradations prone to it.
Silicones have also been reported to improve finishing qualities of the paving mixture.
sections.applicability: Applies when foaming, silo hardening, or truck slumping issues arise in HMA production and handling.

sections.title: Dense-Graded HMA
sections.summary: Introduces dense-graded hot-mix asphalt (HMA), the most common flexible-pavement surfacing: a well-graded aggregate and asphalt cement mixture produced at a central plant, spread to grade with an asphalt spreader, and compacted with steel-wheel and rubber-tire rollers to provide a high-strength, water-resistant, smooth-riding pavement layer.
sections.body: Dense-graded HMA consists of a mixture of well-graded aggregate and asphalt cement. The HMA is produced at a central plant, laid to the desired grade with an asphalt spreader, and compacted with steel wheel and rubber tire rollers. HMA provides a high-strength, water-resistant, smooth riding surface.
key_points: Well-graded aggregate blended with asphalt cement, mixed at a central plant
Placed with an asphalt spreader (paver) and compacted with steel-wheel and rubber-tire rollers
Provides high strength, water resistance, and a smooth riding surface
This section covers aggregate considerations, the Marshall mix design procedure, mixture production control, and significance of mixture-property changes
sections.applicability: Applies to dense-graded HMA surface, intermediate, and base course pavement layers on roads and airfields.

sections.title: Aggregate Considerations
sections.summary: Dense-graded HMA aggregate limits: natural sand capped at 15 percent of combined aggregate weight for high-pressure (airfield) mixtures and 25 percent for roadway (low-pressure) mixtures, both subject to mix-design validation; naturally occurring filler (typically 5-6 percent) is usually adequate; all aggregates must meet the property requirements of paragraph 2-3.2.
sections.body: Dense-graded HMA mixtures have several aggregate requirements and considerations. For airfield mixtures that support high-pressure tires, ensure the percentage of natural sand does not exceed 15 percent of the combined weight of the total aggregate. This percentage is 25 percent for roadway (low-pressure) mixtures, but needs to be validated with the mix design. The amount of filler that exists naturally in aggregates is usually sufficient to produce HMA meeting the mix design but needs to be validated; practical considerations and optimum performance dictate 5 to 6 percent filler, which is almost always available in the aggregates being used. Ensure the aggregates used meet the specification requirements for the aggregate properties discussed in paragraph 2-3.2.
key_points: Natural sand limited to 15 percent of combined aggregate weight for high-pressure (airfield) mixtures
Natural sand limited to 25 percent for roadway (low-pressure) mixtures, pending mix-design validation
Naturally occurring filler is usually adequate; 5-6 percent filler is the typical practical target
Aggregates must meet the property requirements of paragraph 2-3.2
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and proportioning aggregate for dense-graded HMA mix designs.

sections.title: Marshall Mix Design
sections.summary: Header section for the DoD Marshall mix design procedure (with a Superpave gyratory-compaction alternative), covering job mix formula content, specimen preparation, compaction method selection, data tabulation, property/asphalt-content relationships, optimum asphalt content determination, dust/asphalt ratio, moisture susceptibility, and Superpave mix design.
sections.body: DoD uses the Marshall mix design method for dense-graded HMA, with Superpave gyratory-compactor mix design available as an alternative per UFGS 32 12 15.13. This section walks through the contractor-supplied job mix formula, specimen preparation and compaction, data tabulation, the relationship of test properties to asphalt content, and the determination of optimum asphalt content and mix acceptability.
key_points: Marshall method uses a Marshall hammer; Superpave uses a gyratory compactor
Procedures follow the Asphalt Institute's MS-2 and CRD-C649/CRD-C650
Covers JMF requirements, specimen prep, compaction method selection, and data tabulation
Culminates in optimum asphalt content determination and mix acceptability evaluation
sections.applicability: Applies to the laboratory mix-design phase of dense-graded HMA, before plant production begins.

sections.title: Contractor-provided Job Mix Formula (JMF)
sections.summary: Current practice has the contractor design the mixture and develop the JMF for the project's aggregates and asphalt; the contractor supplies verification samples and a JMF package covering gradation, optimum asphalt content, aggregate/filler proportions, binder grade, compactive effort, mixing/compaction temperatures, gradation chart plots, property-vs-asphalt-content plots, aggregate test results, and RAP data if used.
sections.body: Current practice is for the contractor to design the mixture and develop the JMF for the aggregates and asphalt used in the paving project. Supply a sufficient amount of aggregate and asphalt to the contracting officer or representative for possible verification tests, and retain material samples until the project is completed and accepted if verification tests are not performed. The JMF must contain, as a minimum: percent passing each sieve for each aggregate and the combined gradation; optimum asphalt content; percent of each aggregate and mineral filler; asphalt penetration or performance grade; number of hammer blows per side (or gyrations for Superpave); laboratory mixing and compaction temperatures; temperature-viscosity relationship of the asphalt cement; the combined gradation plotted on the 0.45-power chart with nominal maximum size stated; graphical plots of stability, flow, air voids, VMA, and unit weight versus asphalt content; bulk specific gravity and absorption of each aggregate; percent natural sand; coarse and fine aggregate test results (LA abrasion, sulfate soundness, fractured faces, flat/elongated particles, clay lumps, sand equivalent, uncompacted voids); tensile strength ratio and wet/dry results; antistrip agent and amount; all modifiers and amounts; and RAP percentage and properties when used. The JMF is adjusted for plant-produced materials only within specification limits; adjustments beyond those limits require a revised mixture design.
key_points: Contractor designs the mixture and develops the JMF; supplies verification samples to the government
JMF must report gradation, optimum AC content, proportions, binder grade, compactive effort, and temperatures
JMF must include the 0.45-power gradation chart and stability/flow/voids/VMA/unit-weight plots vs. AC content
JMF must report coarse/fine aggregate test results, TSR wet/dry results, antistrip agent, and RAP data if used
JMF adjustments beyond specification limits require a revised mixture design
sections.applicability: Applies to the contractor's job mix formula submittal for dense-graded HMA projects.

sections.title: Procedure
sections.summary: Laboratory-compacted samples are tested for air voids, voids filled with asphalt, and VMA; optimum asphalt content is selected primarily from air voids, with final aggregate blend and asphalt content also weighing relative mix costs. The full specimen-preparation procedure applies directly to mixes with no more than 10 percent of total aggregate retained on the 25 mm (1-inch) sieve.
sections.body: Laboratory tests are conducted on laboratory-compacted samples compacted with the effort identified in the specifications. These samples are tested to identify air voids, voids filled with asphalt, and VMA. Based on these properties (primarily air voids) the optimum asphalt content is selected. A final selection of aggregate blend and asphalt content is based on these data with due consideration to the relative costs of the various mixes. The procedure set forth in paragraph 2-4.2.3 applies directly to all mixes containing not more than 10 percent by weight of total aggregate retained on the 25-millimeter (1-inch) sieve.
key_points: Laboratory-compacted samples are tested for air voids, VFA, and VMA
Optimum asphalt content is selected primarily based on air voids
Final blend/content selection also considers relative mix costs
The 2-4.2.3 specimen procedure applies directly to mixes with <=10 percent retained on the 25 mm (1-in.) sieve
sections.applicability: Applies to the overall laboratory Marshall mix-design test procedure.

sections.title: Preparation of Test Specimens
sections.summary: Materials are selected per section 2-3; an example uses the 19 mm (3/4-in.) maximum high-pressure gradation band (No. 2, 12.5 mm nominal) of Table 2-1. Initial mix design is typically run in a central lab on stockpile samples, with subsequent plant-sample adjustments made in a field lab near the plant; proportioning procedures follow in 2-4.2.3.1 and 2-4.2.3.2.
sections.body: Selection of materials for use in designing the paving mix is addressed in section 2-3. As an example, suppose an aggregate gradation for a hot-mix design is required to meet the requirements of the 19-millimeter (3/4-inch) maximum (high-pressure) aggregate gradation band (gradation No. 2, 12.5 mm [1/2 inch] nominal) shown in Table 2-1. The initial mix design tests are usually conducted in a central testing laboratory on samples of stockpile materials taken by the laboratory; adjustments to the mix design are based on samples taken from the asphalt plant and are usually conducted in a field laboratory near the plant. The procedure for proportioning stockpile samples to produce a blend meeting a specified gradation is outlined in paragraphs 2-4.2.3.1 and 2-4.2.3.2.
key_points: Materials are selected per section 2-3
Worked example uses the 19 mm (3/4-in.) maximum high-pressure gradation band of Table 2-1
Initial mix design testing is done in a central lab on stockpile samples
Plant-sample adjustments are made later in a field laboratory near the plant
tables: Table 2-1: Aggregate Gradations for HMA Pavements
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and proportioning stockpile/bin aggregate samples for Marshall specimen preparation.

sections.title: Proportioning of Stockpile Samples
sections.summary: As a preliminary mixture-design step, the proportions of available stockpiled materials needed to meet the design gradation are determined from sieve analyses of each stockpile, plotted on Figure 2-4 (or a 0.45-power curve per the FHWA/Fuller-Thompson gradation formula); trial-and-error blending of the aggregate fractions, typically 2-3 trials, produces the target blend.
sections.body: As a preliminary step in mixture design and manufacture, determine the proportions of the different available stockpiled materials required to produce the mix design gradation of aggregate. This step determines whether a blend meeting the mix design can be produced and, if so, the proportion of each aggregate to be fed from the cold feeder bins into the dryer. Sieve analyses are conducted on material from each stockpile and plotted graphically in Figure 2-4. An alternative plotting method is the 0.45-power curve, developed in the early 1960s by the FHWA using a formula from a study by Fuller and Thompson: P = 100(d/D)^n, where d is the sieve opening in question, P is the total percent passing that sieve, D is the maximum aggregate size, and n = 0.45. FHWA recommends this chart as part of the hot-mix design process. The four aggregate fractions are combined to produce the desired blend by trial-and-error calculation, normally requiring two or three trials.
key_points: Determines proportions of stockpiled materials needed to meet the design gradation
Sieve analyses per stockpile are plotted graphically (Figure 2-4)
0.45-power gradation curve formula (FHWA/Fuller-Thompson): P = 100(d/D)^n, n = 0.45
Trial-and-error blending of aggregate fractions, typically 2-3 trials
Sets the cold-feeder-bin proportions fed into the dryer
figures: Figure 2-4: Gradation Curves for Stockpile Samples
sections.applicability: Applies to the preliminary laboratory proportioning of stockpiled aggregate for a Marshall mix design.

sections.title: Proportioning of Bin Samples from Batch Plants
sections.summary: Once a workable blend is established from available materials, samples are processed through the asphalt plant for verification (or during test-section construction); hot-bin sieve analyses are plotted on Figure 2-5 and blended to reproduce the JMF gradation, usually within 2-3 trials; this step is unnecessary for drum mix plants since aggregate is not rescreened.
sections.body: Once it is demonstrated that a blend can be prepared from the available materials, samples of these materials are processed through the asphalt plant for verification of the mix design or during construction of the test section. Conduct sieve analyses for each batch of processed aggregate; the data are shown graphically in Figure 2-5. Blend the hot-bin aggregates to produce the same gradation as that produced in the JMF: the percentage of each bin is estimated, calculations determine the gradation produced from those estimated percentages, and the recombined blend's gradation is checked against the desired gradation. Two or three trials are usually sufficient. This step is not needed when a drum mix plant is used since the aggregate is not rescreened in the plant.
key_points: Verifies the mix design blend using plant-processed (hot-bin) aggregate samples
Hot-bin sieve analyses are plotted graphically (Figure 2-5)
Blend percentages are estimated and iterated (2-3 trials typical) to match the JMF gradation
Not required for drum mix plants, since their aggregate is not rescreened
figures: Figure 2-5: Gradation Curves for Bin Samples
sections.applicability: Applies to batch-plant hot-bin aggregate verification during mix design or test-section construction.

sections.title: Asphalt Contents for Specimens
sections.summary: Laboratory tests are run at a minimum of five trial asphalt contents (two above, two below, and one near the estimated optimum), by total mix weight; preliminary work uses 1 percent increments and final design uses 0.5 percent increments.
sections.body: The quantity of asphalt binder required for an aggregate is important to ensure performance. Normally, to start the laboratory tests, an estimate is made of the optimum amount of asphalt binder based on total weight of mix. Laboratory tests usually are conducted for a minimum of five asphalt contents: two above, two below, and one near the estimated optimum asphalt content. Incremental changes of 1 percent of asphalt are used for preliminary work, but increments of 0.5 percent are used for final design.
key_points: Minimum of five trial asphalt contents tested per specimen set
Two contents above, two below, and one near the estimated optimum
1 percent increments for preliminary work
0.5 percent increments for final design
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting the trial asphalt content range for Marshall specimen preparation.

sections.title: Selection of Design Compaction Method
sections.summary: DoD uses the Marshall mix design method (Marshall hammer), with Superpave (gyratory compactor) also available per MS-2/CRD-C649; when using CRD-C649, mixing temperature is set for a binder kinematic viscosity of 280+/-30 centistokes (ASTM D2493). A manual Marshall hammer is preferred for mix design; a mechanical hammer must be calibrated against it, project-specifically, and verified weekly.
sections.body: DoD uses the Marshall mix design method. Specifications have also been prepared for using Superpave mix design procedures with the Superpave Gyratory Compactor. Procedures for the Marshall mix design tests are described in the Asphalt Institute's Manual Series No. 2 (MS-2) and CRD-C649; the primary difference between methods is the compactor (Marshall hammer vs. gyratory compactor). When using CRD-C649, establish the mixing temperature to provide the asphalt binder a kinematic viscosity of 280+/-30 centistokes per ASTM D2493. A manual hammer is required for mix design; when a mechanical hammer is used for full-scale production, calibrate it to produce the same specified density as the manual hammer. Compact plant-produced samples using 50/75 blows as specified with a manual hammer and a variable number of blows with a mechanical hammer, then select the mechanical-hammer blow count that reproduces the manual-hammer density. This correlation is valid for one project only (it varies by mix) and must be verified weekly during the project.
key_points: DoD's standard method is Marshall (Marshall hammer); Superpave (gyratory compactor) is an available alternative
Procedures follow Asphalt Institute MS-2 and CRD-C649
CRD-C649 mixing temperature targets binder viscosity of 280+/-30 centistokes (ASTM D2493)
Manual hammer preferred for mix design; mechanical hammer must be calibrated to match manual-hammer density
Mechanical-hammer calibration is project-specific and must be re-verified weekly
sections.applicability: Applies when choosing and calibrating the Marshall or Superpave compaction method for a project.

sections.title: Tabulation of Data
sections.summary: Specimen test data (stability, flow, unit weight, VTM, VMA, VFA) are tabulated per MS-2/CRD-C649/CRD-C650 forms, following the Table 2-6 arrangement, then plotted vs. asphalt content in Figure 2-6(a-f); desired VMA depends on aggregate particle size per Table 2-7 (referenced from Table 2-6). Unit weight is measured per ASTM D2726 at 25C (77F) and converted to kg/m3 or lb/ft3.
sections.body: After selecting the laboratory design method and preparing test specimens, tabulate the data on forms similar to those shown in MS-2 or CRD-C649 and CRD-C650 for the Marshall procedure and for Superpave. Arranging data as shown in Table 2-6 facilitates tabulation of specimen test property data; other needed material properties include the bulk specific gravity of the aggregate and the specific gravity of the asphalt binder. Make plots of stability, flow, unit weight, percent voids total mix (VTM), percent VMA, and percent voids filled with asphalt (VFA) as shown in Figure 2-6(a-f). The desired VMA values depend on the aggregate particle size, per Table 2-7. Unit weight values are determined per ASTM D2726 in g/cm3 at 25 degrees C (77 degrees F), then converted to kg/m3 (multiply by 997) or lb/ft3 (multiply by 62.24). The stability and flow values are also plotted on Figure 2-6 to evaluate mixture properties (flow and stability are not used for Superpave).
key_points: Specimen data tabulated per MS-2/CRD-C649/CRD-C650 forms, arranged as in Table 2-6
Plots made of stability, flow, unit weight, VTM, VMA, and VFA vs. asphalt content (Figure 2-6a-f)
Desired minimum VMA depends on aggregate particle size (Table 2-7)
Unit weight measured per ASTM D2726 at 25C (77F); convert g/cm3 to kg/m3 (x997) or lb/ft3 (x62.24)
Flow and stability are plotted for Marshall but are not used for Superpave mixes
figures: Figure 2-6(a-f): Asphalt Paving Mix Design for Typical Mix
tables: Table 2-6: Computation of Properties of Asphalt Mixtures
Table 2-7: Minimum Percent Voids in Mineral Aggregate (VMA)
sections.applicability: Applies to tabulating and plotting Marshall/Superpave specimen test data across the trial asphalt-content range.

sections.title: Relationship of Test Properties to Asphalt Cement Content
sections.summary: Test-property curves follow consistent trends for non-modified asphalt (less consistent for polymer-modified binders): flow increases at an increasing rate; stability rises then falls; unit weight peaks slightly past the stability peak; VTM decreases toward a minimum; VMA decreases then rises again as excess asphalt pushes particles apart; VFA increases toward a maximum, mirroring VTM.
sections.body: Test property curves, plotted as described in paragraph 2-4.2.6, have been found to follow a reasonably consistent pattern for mixes made with non-modified grades of asphalt cement; polymer-modified asphalt cements exhibit less consistent trends. Standard trends shown in Figure 2-6(a-f): Flow increases at an increasing rate with increasing asphalt content (Marshall only, not used in Superpave). Marshall stability increases with increasing asphalt content up to a point, then decreases (Marshall only). Unit weight of the total mix follows a curve similar to stability, but peaks at a slightly higher asphalt content. VTM decreases with increasing asphalt content, approaching a minimum void content. VMA decreases with increasing asphalt content as the mix becomes better lubricated and easier to compact, then increases again as excess asphalt pushes aggregate particles apart. VFA increases with increasing asphalt content, approaching a maximum in the same manner VTM approaches a minimum.
key_points: Flow increases at an increasing rate with AC content (Marshall only)
Stability rises then falls with increasing AC content (Marshall only)
Unit weight curve resembles the stability curve but peaks at slightly higher AC content
VTM decreases toward a minimum void content with increasing AC content
VMA decreases (better lubrication) then increases again (excess asphalt pushes particles apart)
VFA increases toward a maximum, mirroring the VTM trend
Polymer-modified binders exhibit less consistent property-vs-AC trends
figures: Figure 2-6(a-f): Asphalt Paving Mix Design for Typical Mix
sections.applicability: Applies when interpreting Marshall/Superpave property-vs-asphalt-content curves to select optimum asphalt content.

sections.title: Requirement for Additional Test Specimens
sections.summary: Erratic test-property data (which complicates curve plotting) is remedied by testing additional specimens at each asphalt content; this section also documents the mixture-property calculation formulas (2-4.2.8.1) and the stability/flow determination procedure with a worked example (2-4.2.8.2).
sections.body: The curves in Figure 2-6 are typical of those normally obtained when non-modified grades of asphalt cement are used with aggregate mixes. Some aggregate blends furnish erratic data that make plotting the typical curves difficult; in these cases, increasing the number of specimens tested at each asphalt content normally results in data that plots as typical curves.
key_points: Erratic property data is addressed by testing more specimens per asphalt content
More specimens typically restore the expected typical-curve shape
Followed by the mixture-property equations (2-4.2.8.1) and stability/flow procedure (2-4.2.8.2)
sections.applicability: Applies when Marshall/Superpave test data is scattered or inconsistent across the trial asphalt-content range.

sections.title: Equations Used for Calculation of Mixture Properties
sections.summary: Defines the Marshall/Superpave mixture-property variables (Gb, Gsb, Pb, Gmb, Gmm, Vv, VMA, VFA, sample weights) and gives the governing formulas: bulk specific gravity of the mixture Gmb = Wdry / (Wssd - Wsubmerged); air voids Vv = 100(1 - Gmb/Gmm); voids in mineral aggregate VMA = 100 - [Gmb(1-Pb)/Gsb]x100; and voids filled with asphalt VFA = 100(VMA - Vv)/VMA.
sections.body: Mixture properties: Gb = specific gravity of binder (ASTM D70); Gsb = bulk specific gravity of aggregate (ASTM C127/C128); Pb = percent of total asphalt by weight; Gmb = bulk specific gravity of mixture (ASTM D2726); Gmm = theoretical maximum specific gravity of mixture (ASTM D2041); Vv = air voids, percent of total mixture; VMA = voids in mineral aggregate, percent of total mixture; VFA = voids filled with asphalt; Wdry = weight of the compacted sample dry; Wsubmerged = weight of the sample submerged in water 3-5 minutes; WSSD = saturated-surface-dry weight after blotting. Governing formulas: bulk specific gravity of mixture, Gmb = Wdry / (WSSD - Wsubmerged); air voids, Vv = 100 x (1 - Gmb/Gmm); voids in mineral aggregate, VMA = 100 - [(Gmb x (1 - Pb)) / Gsb] x 100; voids filled with asphalt, VFA = 100 x (VMA - Vv) / VMA.
key_points: Gmb (bulk specific gravity of mixture) = Wdry / (WSSD - Wsubmerged)
Vv (air voids, %) = 100 x (1 - Gmb/Gmm)
VMA (%) = 100 - [Gmb x (1 - Pb) / Gsb] x 100
VFA (%) = 100 x (VMA - Vv) / VMA
Gb, Gsb, Pb, Gmm are input properties from ASTM D70/C127-C128/D2041 tests; Vv/VMA/VFA are the derived mixture properties

sections.applicability: Applies to computing air voids, VMA, and VFA from Marshall/Superpave specimen weight and specific-gravity measurements.

sections.title: Determination of Stability and Flow
sections.summary: Stability (load to failure) and flow (deformation at failure) are measured per ASTM D6927, with a height correction to an equivalent 6.35 cm (2.5-in.) specimen. A full worked example (Specimen 1 at 5.0% AC, Gb=1.02, Gsb=2.70, Gmm=2.519) carries the Gmb, Vv (3.8%), and VMA (14.8%) calculations from 2-4.2.8.1 through to numeric results.
sections.body: Stability and flow are determined by measuring the load and deformation of a sample at failure (ASTM D6927). The adjusted stability corrects samples taller or shorter than 6.35 cm (2.5 in.) to an equivalent stability for a 6.35 cm (2.5-in.)-tall sample, based on measured height or volume. Worked example: for Specimen No. 1 at 5.0 percent asphalt content in Table 2-6, with binder specific gravity 1.02, aggregate bulk specific gravity 2.70, and theoretical maximum density (Gmm) 2.519 -- sample volume = Wssd - Wsubmerged = 1240.2 - 729.3 = 510.9 cc; bulk specific gravity Gmb = 1237.9 / (1240.2 - 729.3) = 2.423; air voids Vv = 100 x (1 - 2.423/2.519) = 3.8 percent; VMA = 100 - [2.423 x (1 - 0.05) / 2.70] x 100 = 14.8 percent; VFA = 100 x (14.8 - 3.8)/14.7 = 79.6 percent (approximately, per the source rounding).
key_points: Stability = load to failure, flow = deformation at failure, both measured per ASTM D6927
Height-correction adjusts stability of non-standard-height samples to an equivalent 6.35 cm (2.5-in.) sample

Worked example: Gmb = 1237.9 / 510.9 = 2.423
Worked example: Vv = 100 x (1 - 2.423/2.519) = 3.8 percent
Worked example: VMA = 100 - [2.423 x 0.95 / 2.70] x 100 = 14.8 percent; VFA ~ 79.6 percent

sections.title: Importance of Asphalt Content
sections.summary: Optimum asphalt content is a critical factor in meeting the specified paving-mix design; extensive research has produced criteria both for selecting optimum asphalt content for a given aggregate blend and for verifying that the aggregate/asphalt combination furnishes the intended design mix at that optimum content.
sections.body: Previous testing has indicated that optimum asphalt content is an important factor in meeting the specified design of an asphalt paving mixture. Extensive research has resulted in criteria for determining the optimum asphalt content for a given blend of aggregates. Criteria have also been established to determine whether the aggregate furnishes the design paving mix at the selected optimum asphalt content.
key_points: Optimum asphalt content is a critical mix-design factor
Established criteria exist for selecting optimum asphalt content for a given aggregate blend
Separate criteria verify mix acceptability at the selected optimum content
sections.applicability: Applies as the rationale for the optimum-asphalt-content and acceptability procedures that follow.

sections.title: Determination Optimum Asphalt Content & Acceptability of Mix
sections.summary: Optimum asphalt content and mix acceptability are read from the Figure 2-6 property curves against the Table 2-8 design/acceptability criteria (separate criteria for 50- and 75-blow compactive effort). Worked example: optimum AC is set at 4 percent air voids from the VTM curve (Table 2-9, 4.9 percent), and Table 2-10 confirms 4.9 percent AC meets minimum acceptability criteria for 75-blow effort.
sections.body: The data plotted in graphical form in Figure 2-6(a-f) is used to illustrate the determination of optimum asphalt content. In addition to the data from Figure 2-6, optimum asphalt content and acceptability of the mix are determined based on Table 2-8, which gives separate criteria for specimens prepared with 50- or 75-blow compactive efforts. As shown in Table 2-9, the optimum asphalt content is determined at 4 percent air voids for surface or intermediate mixtures, and is determined to be 4.9 percent in the worked example. Table 2-10 shows that at the optimum bitumen content of 4.9 percent, this mixture meets the minimum criteria for acceptability of the mix for a 75-blow compactive effort.
key_points: Optimum AC content and acceptability are read from Figure 2-6 curves against Table 2-8 criteria
Table 2-8 gives separate design/acceptability criteria for 50-blow and 75-blow (or 50/75-gyration) compactive effort
Worked example: optimum AC set at 4 percent air voids (VTM curve) = 4.9 percent (Table 2-9)
Worked example: Table 2-10 confirms 4.9 percent AC meets minimum acceptability criteria for 75-blow effort

sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and confirming the final design optimum asphalt content for a Marshall mix design.

sections.title: Dust/Asphalt Ratio
sections.summary: The dust/asphalt (dust proportion) check is the ratio of aggregate mass passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve to the effective asphalt content, percent of total mix mass; the normal acceptable range is 0.8 to 1.2, balancing adequate stability against excessively low effective asphalt content and durability problems.
sections.body: One check of the design mixture is the dust proportion: the ratio of the mass of aggregate passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve, divided by the effective asphalt content, in percent of total mass of the mixture. The normal range is 0.8 to 1.2. The ratio ensures dust is present in the mix to provide good stability but not so much that it results in excessively low effective asphalt content and subsequent durability problems.
key_points: Dust/asphalt ratio = (mass passing 0.075 mm / No. 200 sieve) / effective asphalt content, percent of total mix mass
Normal acceptable range: 0.8 to 1.2
Too little dust: inadequate stability; too much dust: excessively low effective AC and durability problems
sections.applicability: Applies as a mix-design check on the aggregate fines-to-effective-asphalt-content balance.

sections.title: Moisture Susceptibility
sections.summary: The final mix-design evaluation is a moisture-susceptibility (tensile strength ratio, TSR) test per ASTM D4867 at the selected optimum asphalt content; a TSR below 75 percent requires an antistrip additive in the mixture.
sections.body: The final evaluation of the design mixture involves a test for moisture susceptibility. The TSR of the mixture at the selected optimum is performed according to ASTM D4867. A TSR value of less than 75 percent requires the use of an antistrip additive in the mixture.
key_points: TSR (tensile strength ratio) moisture-susceptibility test per ASTM D4867
Performed at the selected optimum asphalt content
TSR < 75 percent requires an antistrip additive
sections.applicability: Applies as the final moisture-durability check of a completed Marshall (or Superpave) mix design.

sections.title: Superpave Mix Design
sections.summary: Superpave mix design (UFGS 32 12 15.13 option) shares common aggregate/binder requirements with Marshall but compacts larger samples (150 mm dia. x 115 mm tall vs. Marshall's 102 mm x 64 mm) with a gyratory compactor at 75 gyrations (tire pressure >1380 kPa/200 psi) or 50 gyrations (<=1380 kPa); flow and stability are not tested; optimum AC is likewise selected at 4 percent air voids, and gyration counts were calibrated to match Marshall blow counts (75=75, 50=50).
sections.body: Superpave mix design is acceptable for airfield pavements; UFGS 32 12 15.13 provides it as an option. Marshall and Superpave share common aggregate and asphalt binder requirements; the key difference is the compaction method and sample size -- Marshall samples are 102 mm (4 in.) diameter by 64 mm (2.5 in.) tall, compacted with a Marshall hammer, while Superpave samples are 150 mm (6 in.) diameter by 115 mm (4.6 in.) tall, compacted with a Superpave gyratory compactor. The number of gyrations is 75 for high tire pressures above 1380 kPa (200 psi) and 50 for lower tire pressures. Asphalt content is varied in 0.5 percent increments as with Marshall; stability and flow are not tested for Superpave. Air voids, VMA, and VFA specification requirements and determination methods are the same for both methods, and optimum asphalt content is likewise selected at 4 percent air voids, followed by the same moisture-susceptibility testing. The Superpave gyration counts (75/50) were selected to match the corresponding Marshall blow counts (75/50), so the same aggregate is expected to yield the same mix-design result by either method.
key_points: Superpave is an alternative to Marshall for DoD airfield pavements (UFGS 32 12 15.13)
Same aggregate/binder requirements; differs in compactor and sample size
Marshall samples: 102 mm x 64 mm; Superpave samples: 150 mm x 115 mm
Gyrations: 75 for tire pressure >1380 kPa (200 psi), 50 for <=1380 kPa, calibrated to match Marshall blow counts
Stability and flow are not part of the Superpave procedure
Optimum AC content selected at 4 percent air voids, same as Marshall
figures: Figure 2-6(a-f): Asphalt Paving Mix Design for Typical Mix
sections.applicability: Applies when Superpave gyratory mix design is selected as the alternative to Marshall for a project.

sections.title: Mixture Control
sections.summary: Header section for translating the completed JMF into consistent asphalt-plant production: plant laboratory staffing/equipment, the heaviest QC demand at plant startup, routine mix adjustments for hot-bin/drum-plant gradation drift, and the full production/laydown quality control and quality assurance program (2-4.3.4).
sections.body: After the aggregate and asphalt binder quality have been confirmed and the mix design completed, the next step is ensuring the JMF is produced at the asphalt plant. A complete plant laboratory, staffed and equipped per MS-2/CRD-C649/CRD-C650, is required to evaluate produced material quality; because of asphalt plant capacity, at least two technicians should be assigned to conduct control tests so all testing can be completed in a timely manner.
key_points: Requires a fully equipped plant laboratory per MS-2/CRD-C649/CRD-C650
At least two lab technicians recommended given asphalt-plant production capacity
Covers JMF production startup, mix adjustments, and the QC/QA program
sections.applicability: Applies once mix design is complete and asphalt plant production begins.

sections.title: JMF Production at Asphalt Plant
sections.summary: A complete plant laboratory, located at the plant site and equipped per MS-2/CRD-C649/CRD-C650, is required to evaluate produced material quality; assign at least two technicians given typical asphalt-plant production capacity so control testing can be completed in a timely manner.
sections.body: After the aggregate and asphalt binder qualities have been determined to meet the required mix design, the next step is to ensure that the JMF is produced at the asphalt plant. To evaluate the quality of the material produced and ensure the required paving mixture is produced, a complete plant laboratory is required. Locate the laboratory at the plant site and ensure it contains the same equipment as that listed in MS-2 or CRD-C649 and CRD-C650. Because of the capacity of asphalt plants, assign at least two technicians to conduct control tests; otherwise, all testing cannot be completed in a timely manner.
key_points: Plant laboratory located at the plant site, equipped per MS-2/CRD-C649/CRD-C650
At least two technicians recommended to keep pace with plant production capacity
sections.applicability: Applies to staffing and equipping the plant laboratory once JMF production begins.

sections.title: Asphalt Plant Laboratory Burden
sections.summary: Plant laboratory demand peaks at production startup; aggregate/asphalt feed rates and proportions must be held constant, since plant-supplied aggregate gradation often does not exactly reproduce the JMF, requiring slight JMF modification within specification-permitted limits.
sections.body: The heaviest demands on plant laboratory facilities occur at the initiation of plant production. Feed aggregates and asphalt binder through the plant at a relatively constant rate and at the correct proportions. The gradation of the aggregate supplied by the plant often does not precisely reproduce the job mix formula developed in mix design, often requiring the JMF to be modified slightly; the specifications provide guidance on how much the mix may be modified without requiring a new mix design. Feed the aggregates and asphalt binder through the plant at a constant rate to obtain efficient plant operation and produce a mixture conforming to requirements.
key_points: Plant laboratory demand is heaviest at production startup
Aggregate/asphalt must be fed at a constant rate and correct proportions
Plant gradation often requires slight JMF modification, within specification limits
Modifications beyond specification limits require a new mix design
sections.applicability: Applies during asphalt plant production startup and ongoing feed-rate control.

sections.title: Mix Adjustments
sections.summary: Batch-plant hot-bin and drum-mixer aggregate gradations cannot exactly reproduce the laboratory design gradation (fines are generated during handling/production); usually only slight JMF adjustments are needed, but a substantial gradation shift that prevents meeting the JMF requires redesigning the mix with plant-produced aggregates and re-running the full specimen test/acceptability procedure.
sections.body: The aggregates obtained from the hot bins of batch plants cannot be proportioned to exactly reproduce the gradation of the aggregate used in the laboratory design; similarly, drum-mixer plant aggregate gradation does not entirely duplicate the mixture-design gradation, because fines are generated during handling and production operations. Usually only slight adjustments to the original mix design are required and a completely new design is not needed. If the gradation change is substantial enough to prevent the contractor from meeting the JMF, it is necessary to adjust or redesign the mix using plant-produced aggregates; specimens for the new design are prepared and tested in the same manner as the original design, and the optimum asphalt content and mix acceptability are re-determined.
key_points: Plant aggregate gradation never exactly matches the laboratory design gradation (fines generated in handling)
Usually only slight JMF adjustments are needed, not a full redesign
Substantial gradation shifts require redesigning with plant-produced aggregate
Redesign specimens are prepared/tested using the same procedure as the original design
sections.applicability: Applies when plant-produced aggregate gradation drifts from the laboratory job mix formula.

sections.title: Production & Laydown Quality Control & Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Sets out the full QC (contractor) and QA (owner) testing program for HMA production and laydown -- asphalt content, gradation, temperatures, moisture, voids, VMA, stability/flow, density, grade, and smoothness -- with statistical lot/sublot evaluation; sub-topics (2-4.3.4.1 - 2-4.3.4.6) cover QA methodology, QC methodology, deviation-from-JMF calculations, density measurement, grade/smoothness evaluation, and control charts.
sections.body: Control several items routinely during production and laydown to provide the specified pavement. As part of quality control, test for and control at minimum: asphalt content, aggregate gradation, temperatures, aggregate moisture, moisture in the asphalt mixture, laboratory air voids, VMA, stability, flow, in-place density, grade, and smoothness. As part of quality assurance, test mixture items (aggregate gradation, asphalt content, voids, VMA) and laydown items (density, smoothness, final grade); measure and analyze these items statistically. When items fail to meet specified requirements, the contract unit price is reduced or the mixture is rejected; projects under 1,000 metric tons of hot-mix are constructed without the pay-reduction clause for economic reasons.
key_points: QC tests: asphalt content, gradation, temperatures, moisture, air voids, VMA, stability, flow, density, grade, smoothness
QA tests: mixture items (gradation, AC, voids, VMA) and laydown items (density, smoothness, final grade), evaluated statistically
Non-conforming lots trigger a pay reduction or mixture rejection
Projects under 1,000 metric tons (1,000 tons) hot-mix are exempt from the pay-reduction clause
sections.applicability: Applies to the statistical quality control/quality assurance program during HMA production and paving.

sections.title: QA Methodology
sections.summary: Work is divided into lots (each independently evaluated, capped at 2,000 metric tons or one normal day's production), subdivided into four equal sublots; a random sample per sublot (uncompacted mix, joint core, compacted-HMA core) is taken per ASTM D3665 sampling-location guidance; a worked example locates a random core within a sublot from two random numbers applied to lane length and width.
sections.body: To evaluate the quality of a job, the work is divided into lots, each considered a separate job and evaluated solely on its own test results. A lot does not exceed 2,000 metric tons (2,000 tons) of production or one normal day's production. Subdivide the lot into four equal sublots and take a random sample from each sublot to evaluate air voids, asphalt content, and density: one sample of uncompacted asphalt mixture, one field core from a pavement joint area, and one field core from the compacted HMA. ASTM D3665 provides detailed guidance on determining sampling locations within a sublot. Worked example: for a 1,000-metric-ton lot placed in two lanes (2,000 m and 1,000 m long, 3 m wide, 1,000 m of joint length), one joint sample is taken per 250 m of joint length and one mat sample per 750 m of paving; with random numbers 0.108 and 0.485, the core location from the sublot start is 750 m x 0.108 = 81 m along, and 2.7 m x 0.485 = 1.31 m from 0.3 m inside the pavement edge.
key_points: Lot capped at 2,000 metric tons (2,000 tons) or one normal day's production
Each lot subdivided into four equal sublots
One random sample per sublot: uncompacted mix, joint core, and compacted-HMA core
Sampling locations follow ASTM D3665 guidance
Worked example converts two random numbers (0.108, 0.485) into a core location within the sublot
sections.applicability: Applies to quality-assurance lot/sublot division and random sample-location selection.

sections.title: QC Methodology
sections.summary: Asphalt content and gradation are determined from samples taken between production and laydown, preferably from the back of loaded trucks at the plant (not from the paver hopper/auger, which is unsafe and impractical); for a 1,000-metric-ton lot, one sample per 250 metric tons is taken at a randomly selected production count.
sections.body: The asphalt content and aggregate gradation are determined from samples of the asphalt mix taken between the production and laydown operation. Samples are preferably taken from the back of loaded trucks before they leave the asphalt plant; sampling from truck at the laydown site or from behind the paver is also acceptable, but taking samples from the paver hopper or auger during production is not acceptable, since it is unsafe and difficult to obtain a valid sample. ASTM D979 and D3665 provide guidance on obtaining samples. If a 1,000-metric-ton (1,000-ton) lot is selected, a sample is taken for each 250 metric tons (250 tons) produced, at a randomly selected production count (e.g., a random number between 1 and 250 determines that the 200th ton batched is sampled).
key_points: AC content and gradation sampled between production and laydown
Preferred sampling point: back of loaded trucks at the plant
Sampling from the paver hopper/auger during production is not acceptable (unsafe, unreliable)
Sampling guidance from ASTM D979 and D3665
For a 1,000-ton lot, one sample per 250 tons, at a randomly selected production count
sections.applicability: Applies to contractor quality-control sampling of asphalt content and gradation during production.

sections.title: Air Void and Asphalt Content Deviations from JMF
sections.summary: The four sublot air-void and asphalt-content results are each compared to the JMF and their absolute differences averaged to a mean absolute deviation, which sets the maximum percent payment per the specification's payment tables; a worked example (air voids 3.5, 3.0, 4.0, 3.7 vs. 4.0 design) yields a mean absolute deviation of 0.45.
sections.body: After the four asphalt contents and corresponding void values are determined for a lot, these results are compared with the JMF and the absolute difference is determined. Worked example: if the design air void content is 4.0 percent and the four sampled air void contents are 3.5, 3.0, 4.0, and 3.7 percent, the mean absolute deviation from the JMF is (0.5+1.0+0.0+0.3)/4 = 0.45. The same procedure determines the mean absolute deviation for asphalt content. After the mean absolute deviations are determined for air void content and asphalt content, the maximum percent payment for the lot is determined from the specification's payment tables.
key_points: Mean absolute deviation = average of |sublot result - JMF value| across the 4 sublots
Worked example (air voids): deviations 0.5, 1.0, 0.0, 0.3 from a 4.0 percent design value average to 0.45
Same procedure applies to asphalt content deviation
Mean absolute deviations for voids and AC content set the lot's maximum percent payment (per specification tables)
sections.applicability: Applies to computing pay-factor deviations of lot air-void and asphalt-content results from the JMF.

sections.title: Density Measurements
sections.summary: Mat and joint density are measured from pavement cores (not density gauges) per ASTM D3665/D5361, expressed as a percentage of theoretical maximum density (TMD); a worked example averages four sublot TMD/mat-density/joint-density values to compute mat lot density (97.8%) and average joint density (96.8%), used with specification pay tables.
sections.body: Determine density within the mat and at the joints between mats; density measurements for acceptance are taken from cores, not density gauges. Obtain one sample in the mat and one in the joint for each sublot, per ASTM D3665 location guidance; ASTM D5361 covers obtaining the pavement sample. Mat and joint density for each sublot are expressed as a percentage of TMD for that sublot (a joint core spanning two sublots uses the average TMD of both). Worked example: for four sublots with TMDs 2,408 / 2,398 / 2,389 / 2,421 kg/m3 (average 2,404 kg/m3) and mat densities 2,324 / 2,356 / 2,348 / 2,373 kg/m3, mat lot density = (2,324+2,356+2,348+2,373)/[4x2,404] = 97.8 percent; with joint densities 2,311 / 2,324 / 2,343 / 2,325 kg/m3, average joint density = 96.8 percent. These averages, with specification pay tables, set the lot's maximum percent payment.
key_points: Density measured from pavement cores only (density gauges not acceptable for acceptance)
One mat sample and one joint sample per sublot, per ASTM D3665/D5361
Density expressed as percent of theoretical maximum density (TMD); joint-spanning cores use the average TMD of both sublots
Worked example: mat lot density = 97.8 percent, average joint density = 96.8 percent, from 4-sublot data
Density results feed the specification's maximum-percent-payment tables
sections.applicability: Applies to acceptance-testing mat and joint density of placed HMA pavement.

sections.title: Evaluation of Grade and Smoothness
sections.summary: Completed pavement surface is systematically evaluated for grade and smoothness acceptability, with results compared against specification requirements to determine percent payment.
sections.body: The surface of the completed pavement is evaluated on a systematic basis to determine the acceptability of grade and smoothness. The results are compared with the specification requirements to determine the percent payment for grade and smoothness.
key_points: Completed pavement surface is systematically checked for grade and smoothness
Results are compared against specification requirements
Grade/smoothness results determine percent payment
sections.applicability: Applies to final pavement surface acceptance for grade and smoothness.

sections.title: Quality Control Charts
sections.summary: Control charts (individual values and 4-sample running average) are maintained for critical gradation sieves (No. 4 and No. 200) and for asphalt content, laboratory density, stability, flow, VTM, VFA, mat density, and joint density; a worked mat-density example (Table 2-11, Figure 2-7) shows an out-of-control first result triggering roller-weight/pressure corrections, then in-range results.
sections.body: To properly evaluate quality control and maintain up-to-date records of test results, maintain control charts, recommended for the critical gradation sieves (4.75 mm/No. 4 and 75 micrometers/No. 200), as well as for asphalt content, laboratory density, stability, flow, VTM, VFA, mat density, and joint density; plot both individual values and the running average of four samples. Worked example (Table 2-11 density data, Figure 2-7 control chart): the first mat-density test result fell below the desired range, so the process was judged out of control and operations stopped until the cause was identified. Corrections (rubber-tired roller weight increased from 18 to 22.5 metric tons, tire pressure increased from 480 to 620 kPa) brought later results into the desired range, and the four-sample moving average smoothed the plotted values to make trends easier to spot.
key_points: Control charts recommended for critical sieves (No. 4, No. 200) plus AC content, density, stability, flow, VTM, VFA
Both individual values and a 4-sample running average are plotted
Worked example (Table 2-11 / Figure 2-7): an out-of-range first result triggered a stop-work and process correction
Correction in the example: roller weight raised 18->22.5 metric tons, tire pressure raised 480->620 kPa
Running average smooths individual-value scatter to make trends easier to spot
tables: Table 2-11: Lot Density as a Percent of Laboratory Density
sections.applicability: Applies to ongoing statistical process control of HMA production/laydown test results.

sections.title: Significance of Changes in Mixture Properties
sections.summary: Most QC results (air voids, VMA, AC content, gradation) are quick, reliable indicators of plant-mix consistency; a measurable shift or out-of-spec result signals a mixture problem, usually diagnosed from control charts. Faulty batch-plant scales/operator weighing errors are common causes; drum-mix-plant problems usually trace to incorrect material feed rates. Figure 2-8 catalogs other probable causes.
sections.body: As a general rule, most of the QC test results (for example, air voids, VMA, asphalt content, gradation) are obtainable quickly and are reasonably reliable indicators of the consistency of the plant-produced mix. A measurable change in these properties or properties outside the specified limits indicates a mixture problem; a review of the control charts normally indicates the problem. Adjust mix proportions whenever any test property consistently falls outside the specified tolerances. For batch plants, faulty scales and operator failure to accurately weigh required material proportions are common causes of paving-mixture deficiencies and must be detected readily through close checking of load weights; Figure 2-8 lists other probable causes. For drum mix plants, a mixture problem typically indicates an incorrect feed rate of one or more materials into the plant.
key_points: QC results (voids, VMA, AC content, gradation) are fast, reliable indicators of mix consistency
Out-of-spec or shifting properties signal a mixture problem, usually diagnosed via control charts
Batch plants: faulty scales / operator weighing errors are common deficiency causes
Drum mix plants: mixture problems usually trace to incorrect material feed rates
Figure 2-8 catalogs additional probable causes of HMA mixture deficiencies
figures: Figure 2-8: Types of HMA Deficiencies and Probable Causes
sections.applicability: Applies to diagnosing the root cause when HMA production QC results drift or fall out of specification.

sections.title: Hot-bin Gradations
sections.summary: When batch plants are used, hot-bin gradation tests are run at least once daily during operation, on all bins, in conjunction with pavement mixture sampling, with washed sieve analyses run initially.
sections.body: When batch plants are used, conduct the hot-bin gradation tests at least once daily during operation. Determine hot-bin gradations on all bins in conjunction with sampling of the pavement mixture. Determine washed sieve analyses initially.
key_points: Hot-bin gradation tested at least once daily during batch-plant operation
Tested on all bins, coordinated with pavement mixture sampling
Washed sieve analyses run initially
sections.applicability: Applies to daily quality-control gradation testing at batch-type HMA plants.

sections.title: Construction Control
sections.summary: Well-designed mixes are field-rolled to about 98 percent or more of laboratory-compacted specimen density (or at least 94 percent of theoretical maximum density); intermediate, base, and surface course mixes are rolled until the specified density is achieved.
sections.body: Well-designed mixes are compacted by adequate field rolling to about 98 percent or greater of the density obtained by compacting specimens with previously specified laboratory procedures (or at least 94 percent of theoretical maximum density). Roll asphalt intermediate, base course, or surface course mixes until the density specified is met.
key_points: Field density target: about 98 percent or more of laboratory-compacted density
Equivalent minimum: about 94 percent of theoretical maximum density
Applies to intermediate, base, and surface course HMA mixes
sections.applicability: Applies to field rolling/compaction control targets for placed HMA layers.

sections.title: Pavement Sampling
sections.summary: Density/thickness samples are cored (>=100 mm/4-in. barrel, or 150 mm/6-in. for layers under 50 mm/2-in.) or saw-cut, covering the full layer thickness; daily-production samples must reach the project laboratory by noon the following day with density determined by end of day, so placement adjustments can be made promptly.
