sections.body: Take samples for determining pavement density and thickness either with a coring machine (core barrel nominal diameter of at least 100 millimeters (4 inches)) or by cutting out a section of pavement at least 100 millimeters (4 inches) square with a concrete saw. When the compacted thickness of the pavement is less than 50 millimeters (2 inches), use a 150-millimeter (6-inch)-diameter core barrel. Ensure samples include the entire thickness of the layer being evaluated. Take density samples of each day's production, deliver them to the project laboratory by noon of the following day, and make density determinations by the end of that day; make any needed changes in placing technique immediately prior to placing additional pavement.
key_points: Core barrel >=100 mm (4 in.), or 150 mm (6 in.) for layers under 50 mm (2 in.) compacted thickness
Alternative: saw-cut section at least 100 mm (4 in.) square
Samples must span the full layer thickness being evaluated
Daily-production samples delivered to the lab by noon the next day; density determined by end of day
Placement-technique changes are made immediately, before further paving
sections.applicability: Applies to coring/sawing procedures for pavement density and thickness acceptance samples.

sections.title: Testing Pavement Samples
sections.summary: Samples are trimmed of foreign matter/damaged edges, thickness-measured, and layer-split (chisel or table saw) before density testing (weigh in air and water, per 2-4.2.6/2-4.2.8); damaged samples are discarded and replaced. Nondestructive (nuclear) gauges are fast but affected by thickness, underlying-material density, moisture, and surface smoothness -- useful for roller-pattern development but not for acceptance testing, which requires core samples.
sections.body: Prepare pavement samples for testing by carefully removing all particles of base material or other foreign matter, and trimming broken or damaged edges of sawed samples. Take thickness measurements before separating the sample into layers; split a sample consisting of an intermediate course and surface course at the interface before testing, usually with a few blows of a sharp-edged chisel, or with a concrete table saw when the underlying surface was milled or the asphalt was placed directly on crushed stone base. Eliminating excess tack, uncoated aggregate, and voids from the bottom of a core sample greatly increases the accuracy of density measurements. Determine density of sawed samples by weighing in air and in water, as described in paragraphs 2-4.2.6 and 2-4.2.8; discard and replace samples with apparent damage. Nuclear gauges and other nondestructive density tests are fast but often questionable, being affected by asphalt mixture thickness, underlying-material density, moisture, and test-location smoothness; they are useful for developing roller patterns, but acceptance density testing requires removed samples weighed in air and water.
key_points: Samples are cleaned of foreign matter, trimmed, and thickness-measured before layer separation
Layer separation via chisel blows or a concrete table saw at the course interface
Density determined by weighing dry, submerged, and SSD, per the 2-4.2.6/2-4.2.8 procedure
Damaged samples are discarded and replaced with new samples from the same sublot
Nondestructive nuclear gauges are useful for roller-pattern development but NOT for acceptance testing
sections.applicability: Applies to preparing and testing cored/sawed pavement samples for density acceptance.

sections.title: Density Data
sections.summary: Pavement sample density (measured per 2-4.2.6/2-4.2.8) is compared against the average laboratory density or theoretical maximum density for the same lot to evaluate compaction adequacy.
sections.body: Density data obtained from specimens in the manner described in paragraphs 2-4.2.6 and 2-4.2.8 is compared with the average laboratory density or theoretical maximum density for the same lot.
key_points: Pavement sample density is measured per the 2-4.2.6/2-4.2.8 procedure
Compared against the lot's average laboratory density or theoretical maximum density
sections.applicability: Applies to comparing field pavement density results against the lot's laboratory reference density.

sections.title: Pavement Imperfections and Probable Causes
sections.summary: Pavement imperfections result from deviating from specified laying/rolling operations, not meeting the specified mix design, or faulty plant operation, and are controlled through inspection; Figure 2-9 catalogs the potential HMA pavement imperfections and their probable causes.
sections.body: Pavement imperfections result from not following specified laying and rolling operations as well as not meeting specified mix designs or faulty plant operation. These imperfections are controlled only by inspection. Figure 2-9 presents these potential pavement imperfections and their probable causes.
key_points: Imperfections arise from deviations in laying/rolling, mix design non-conformance, or faulty plant operation
Inspection is the primary control for pavement imperfections
Figure 2-9 catalogs the imperfection types and probable causes
figures: Figure 2-9: Types of HMA Pavement Imperfections and Probable Causes
sections.applicability: Applies to diagnosing visible HMA pavement surface imperfections after construction.

sections.title: Porous Friction Course
sections.summary: Introduces the porous friction course (PFC), an open-graded, free-draining asphalt overlay (equivalent to OGFC) placed on sound existing pavement to reduce hydroplaning and improve wet-weather skid resistance. Covers finished thickness (19-25 mm), use restrictions, and its declining recent use on DoD airfields due to performance/FOD concerns.
sections.body: A PFC is an open-graded, free-draining asphalt paving mixture that is placed on an existing pavement to minimize hydroplaning and to improve skid resistance in wet weather. PFC is just another name for open-graded friction course (OGFC) used by many state DOT agencies. Do not use this surface for low-speed applications or in areas subjected to tank traffic. The thickness of the finished course varies from approximately 19 millimeters (3/4 inch) to 25 millimeters (1 inch). A PFC has a coarse surface texture and is sufficiently porous to permit drainage of water internally as well as along the surface. A combination of water pressure relief through the internal and surface voids and the rough surface texture promotes tire-to-aggregate contact. PFC paving mixtures are produced in HMA plants and placed with conventional asphalt paving machines. Place them on pavements that are in good condition. Similar to Section 2-1.2, determine if a leveling course is required to achieve the desired surface conditions before construction of the PFC. Due to performance issues, FOD potential, PFCs have not been used on airfields in recent years.
key_points: PFC = open-graded, free-draining mixture placed over an existing pavement to reduce hydroplaning and improve wet-weather skid resistance; same product state DOTs call OGFC
Not for low-speed applications or areas subjected to tank traffic
Finished course thickness: approximately 19 mm (3/4 in.) to 25 mm (1 in.)
Internal and surface porosity plus coarse texture relieve water pressure at the tire-pavement interface and improve tire-to-aggregate contact
Produced in standard HMA plants, placed with conventional paving equipment, only over pavements in good condition; a leveling course may be needed first (see 2-1.2)
Due to performance issues and FOD (foreign object debris) potential, PFCs have seen little recent DoD airfield use
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and specifying an open-graded porous friction course overlay for wet-weather skid resistance on pavements in good condition; not applicable to low-speed or tank-traffic areas, and rarely used on current DoD airfields.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Umbrella heading for the two PFC material categories: aggregates (2-5.1.1), which must be highly crushed and abrasion-resistant, and asphalt cement (2-5.1.2), which is normally polymer modified. Detailed acceptance criteria are given in the following two subsections.
key_points: PFC materials are covered in two subsections: aggregates (2-5.1.1) and asphalt cement (2-5.1.2)
PFC requires higher-quality, more highly crushed aggregate than conventional dense-graded HMA
Polymer modified asphalt cement is the norm for PFC to resist draindown and oxidation
sections.applicability: Serves as the material-requirements umbrella for PFC mix design; consult 2-5.1.1 and 2-5.1.2 for specific aggregate and asphalt cement criteria.

sections.title: Aggregates
sections.summary: Sets PFC aggregate quality requirements: maximum LA abrasion loss of 25 or 40 percent depending on tire pressure loading, minimum crushed-face percentages, mandatory antistripping treatment of both the PFC and underlying HMA layer, and gradation per Table 2-12.
sections.body: High-quality aggregates are required for PFCs with a maximum Los Angeles (LA) abrasion loss (ASTM C131) of 25 percent and 40 percent for high and low tire pressure loadings, respectively. A crushed aggregate is required and has a minimum of 90 percent by total weight of aggregate with one crushed face and 70 percent with two crushed faces. Specify antistrip agents when required. Design, specify and use an antistripping agent not only in the PFC but also in the underlying HMA layer regardless of the results from the TSR test (ASTM D4867/D4867M). Table 2-12 presents the aggregate gradation requirements for PFCs.
key_points: Max LA abrasion loss (ASTM C131): 25 percent for high tire pressure loadings, 40 percent for low tire pressure loadings
Crushed aggregate required: minimum 90 percent by weight with one crushed face, minimum 70 percent with two crushed faces
Antistripping agent is specified in BOTH the PFC and the underlying HMA layer regardless of TSR test (ASTM D4867/D4867M) results
Table 2-12 gives the PFC aggregate gradation requirements (Gradations A and B)
tables: Table 2-12: Aggregate Gradation for PFCs
sections.applicability: Governs aggregate quality, crushing, gradation, and antistrip treatment selection for porous friction course mixtures.

sections.title: Asphalt Cement
sections.summary: Specifies PFC asphalt cement test standards (ASTM D946, D3381, D6373, or AASHTO M320) and requires polymer modification to help hold aggregate in place and reduce oxidation deterioration in the porous mat.
sections.body: Test requirements for asphalt cements are outlined in specifications (ASTM D946, D3381, D6373, or AASHTO M320). Guidance on the selection of an asphalt type is provided in section 2-3.1. Historically, many PFCs were constructed using modified asphalt to improve the ability of the asphalt to hold the aggregate in place and reduce oxidation deterioration in the porous mat. When using PFC, specify polymer modified asphalt cement.
key_points: Asphalt cement tested per ASTM D946, D3381, D6373, or AASHTO M320; asphalt type selection guidance is in section 2-3.1
Polymer modified asphalt cement is specified for PFC to hold aggregate in place and reduce oxidation deterioration in the porous mat
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and specifying the asphalt cement grade/type for PFC mixtures.

sections.title: Mixture Design
sections.summary: Umbrella heading covering the five elements of PFC mixture design: aggregate proportioning, fiber stabilizer selection, optimum asphalt content determination, the Kc surface-area factor, and mixing temperature control, detailed in the following subsections.
key_points: PFC mixture design is covered across five subsections: proportioning (2-5.2.1), fiber stabilizers (2-5.2.2), asphalt content (2-5.2.3), Kc factor (2-5.2.4), and mixing temperature (2-5.2.5)
Design centers on combining polymer modified asphalt and fiber to control draindown while meeting a target asphalt content derived from aggregate surface properties
sections.applicability: Serves as the mixture-design umbrella for PFC; consult the following subsections for specific proportioning, stabilizer, asphalt content, and temperature criteria.

sections.title: Proportioning of Aggregates
sections.summary: Directs the use of polymer modified asphalt and fiber together in PFC to reduce draindown during short-term storage and haul, with aggregate gradation selected from Table 2-12.
sections.body: For PFC use polymer modified asphalt and fibers. The modified asphalt and fibers help to reduce draindown when storing for a short period of time and during haul to the paving site. Select the aggregate gradation from Table 2-12.
key_points: PFC mix design uses polymer modified asphalt plus fibers together to control draindown during short-term storage and haul
Aggregate gradation is selected from Table 2-12 (Gradation A or B)
tables: Table 2-12: Aggregate Gradation for PFCs
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting the target aggregate gradation and confirming the polymer-asphalt/fiber combination during PFC mixture proportioning.

sections.title: Fiber Stabilizers
sections.summary: Gives PFC fiber stabilizer requirements: property/test tables for cellulose (Table 2-13) and mineral (Table 2-14) fibers, typical dosage rates of 0.3 and 0.4 percent by mix weight respectively, and a ±10 percent dosage tolerance.
sections.body: Tables 2-13 and 2-14 provide the requirements and test procedures to be used with cellulose and mineral fibers, respectively. The dosage rates normally used for cellulose fibers is 0.3 percent by weight of the total mix and for mineral fibers is 0.4 percent by weight of the total mix. The recommended tolerance for the fibers is 10 percent of the required fiber weight.
key_points: Table 2-13 (cellulose fiber) and Table 2-14 (mineral fiber) give property/test requirements for PFC fiber stabilizers
Typical dosage: 0.3 percent by weight of total mix for cellulose fibers, 0.4 percent for mineral fibers
Fiber dosage tolerance: plus or minus 10 percent of the required fiber weight
tables: Table 2-13: Properties of Cellulose Fibers
Table 2-14: Properties of Mineral Fibers
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting fiber type and dosage rate to control asphalt draindown in a PFC mixture.

sections.title: Asphalt Content
sections.summary: Describes determining optimum PFC asphalt content (EOA) from the Kc surface-area constant (CKE test, ASTM D5148) via EOA = 2Kc+4.0, valid for aggregate specific gravity 2.60-2.80 and absorption below 2.50 percent, with adjustments outside those ranges.
sections.body: The asphalt content of PFCs is expressed as a percentage of the total mix by weight. A surface area constant, Kc, as described in the centrifuge kerosene equivalent (CKE) test (ASTM D5148), is used to determine the optimum asphalt content. The Kc value is used in the relation 2Kc+4.0 to determine the estimate of asphalt (EOA). This asphalt content is valid for aggregates with an apparent specific gravity in the range of 2.60 to 2.80 and with a water absorption value less than 2.50 percent when tested by ASTM C127 for coarse aggregate and ASTM C128 for fine aggregate. A slight increase in asphalt content (up to 0.5 percent) is required when the absorption is greater than 2.50 percent. The EOA is inversely proportional to the specific gravity of the aggregate, ensure adjustments are made when the specific gravity is outside of the 2.60 to 2.80 range.
key_points: Asphalt content is percent of total mix by weight, set from the surface-area constant Kc (CKE test, ASTM D5148) via the relation EOA = 2Kc + 4.0
Relation is valid for aggregate apparent specific gravity 2.60-2.80 and water absorption under 2.50 percent (ASTM C127 coarse / C128 fine)
Absorption greater than 2.50 percent requires up to a 0.5 percent increase in asphalt content
EOA is inversely proportional to aggregate specific gravity; adjust the estimate when specific gravity falls outside the 2.60-2.80 range
sections.applicability: Applies to determining and adjusting the optimum PFC asphalt content (EOA) from the Kc surface-area constant and aggregate specific gravity/absorption.

sections.title: Kc Factor
sections.summary: Defines the Kc factor (relative particle roughness/surface capacity) as determined from percent SAE 10 oil retained on the 9.5 mm x 4.75 mm aggregate fraction per ASTM D5148, with a specific-gravity-based correction to oil retained outside 2.60-2.70.
sections.body: The Kc factor indicates the relative particle roughness and surface capacity based on the porosity of the aggregate to be used for the PFC. The Kc factor is determined from the percent of Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) 10 oil retained, which represents the total effect of the coarse aggregate's absorptive properties and surface roughness. The Kc factor is determined from that portion of the aggregate sample that passes the 9.5-millimeter (3/8-inch) sieve and is retained on the 4.75-millimeter (No. 4) sieve using the procedure described in ASTM D5148. If the specific gravity for the aggregate is greater than 2.70 or less than 2.60, apply a correction to oil retained using the formula given in ASTM D5148. No correction need be applied for asphalt viscosity.
key_points: Kc represents relative particle roughness and surface capacity resulting from aggregate porosity
Determined from percent SAE 10 oil retained by the aggregate fraction passing the 9.5 mm sieve and retained on the 4.75 mm (No. 4) sieve, per ASTM D5148
Specific gravity outside the 2.60-2.70 range requires an oil-retained correction per the ASTM D5148 formula
No correction is required for asphalt viscosity
sections.applicability: Applies to laboratory determination of the Kc surface-area constant used to set PFC asphalt content.

sections.title: Mixing Temperature
sections.summary: Sets PFC mixing temperature to achieve an asphalt viscosity of 275+/-25 centistokes, established from a temperature-viscosity curve (minimum 3 temperatures, ASTM D2170/D2171) plotted per ASTM D2493.
sections.body: Mixing temperature to provide an asphalt viscosity of 275±25 centistokes is obtained by evaluating the temperature-viscosity relationship for the type of asphalt selected at a minimum of three temperatures (ASTM D2170 and ASTM D2171). ASTM D2493 provides details for plotting this information on a graph with temperature versus log viscosity. Plotting this information normally results in a straight-line relationship, and the temperature for the correct viscosity is chosen from the graph.
key_points: Target mixing viscosity for PFC: 275 plus or minus 25 centistokes
Temperature-viscosity relationship is established from at least 3 temperatures per ASTM D2170/D2171
ASTM D2493 plotting procedure (temperature vs. log viscosity) typically yields a straight line used to read off the correct mixing temperature
sections.applicability: Applies to setting the plant mixing temperature for a given PFC asphalt cement source.

sections.title: Plant Control
sections.summary: Umbrella heading for PFC plant quality-control practice: plant laboratory setup, sieve analysis, asphalt content testing, mix-proportion adjustment, and production-control sampling, detailed in the following subsections.
key_points: PFC plant control is covered across five subsections: plant laboratory (2-5.3.1), sieve analysis (2-5.3.2), asphalt content tests (2-5.3.3), mix proportions (2-5.3.4), and controlling plant production (2-5.3.5)
Core purpose is verifying that gradation and asphalt content stay within the job mix formula during production
sections.applicability: Serves as the plant quality-control umbrella for PFC production; consult the following subsections for specific test methods and sampling frequency.

sections.title: Plant Laboratory
sections.summary: Requires a plant laboratory located at the plant to verify aggregate gradation and asphalt binder percentage, minimizing the time between production and testing.
sections.body: A plant laboratory is needed to ensure that the aggregate is properly graded and the mix contains the prescribed percentage of asphalt binder. Locate the laboratory at the plant to minimize the time between production and testing.
key_points: A plant laboratory verifies aggregate gradation and asphalt binder percentage during PFC production
Locate the laboratory at the plant to minimize the time between production and testing
sections.applicability: Applies to plant quality-control organization for PFC production.

sections.title: Sieve Analysis
sections.summary: Specifies ASTM C136 sieve analysis using a defined sieve set (19 mm down to 75 um), sampled from hot bins for batch plants or cold feeds for drum mixers, plus gradation checks on aggregate recovered from the finished mixture.
sections.body: Conduct all sieve analyses by the method described in ASTM C136. Recommended sieve sizes for plant sieve analysis are: 19 millimeter (3/4 inch), 12.5 millimeter (1/2 inch), 9.5 millimeter (3/8 inch), 4.75 millimeter (No. 4), 2.36 millimeter (No. 8), 600 micrometers (No. 30), and 75 micrometers (No. 200). For batch-mix plants, accomplish sieve analyses on material from each plant hot bin. Obtain samples for these sieve analyses after a few tons of aggregate have been processed through the dryer and screens so that the sample is representative. For drum mixers, make the sieve analysis directly from the cold feeds. Final mix proportions are determined on the basis of these analyses. For both types of plants, aggregate gradations will also be conducted on the aggregate recovered from the asphalt mixture.
key_points: Sieve analysis per ASTM C136 using sieves 19, 12.5, 9.5, 4.75, 2.36 mm, 600 um, and 75 um
Batch plants: sample each hot bin after a few tons have passed through the dryer/screens so the sample is representative
Drum mixers: sample directly from the cold feeds
Gradation is also checked on aggregate recovered from the finished asphalt mixture, for both plant types
sections.applicability: Applies to routine plant gradation control for both batch-mix and drum-mix PFC plants.

sections.title: Asphalt Content Tests
sections.summary: Covers PFC asphalt content test methods: extraction (ASTM D2172), calibrated nuclear gauge (ASTM D4125), and ignition (ASTM D6307), plus ASTM D5444 gradation on recovered aggregate; notes the nuclear gauge method precludes aggregate recovery.
sections.body: Accomplish extraction tests in accordance with ASTM D2172. A nuclear gauge is used to determine the asphalt content, when tested in accordance with ASTM D4125, provided the gauge is calibrated. The asphalt content is also determined by the ignition method in accordance with ASTM D6307. Follow procedures specified in ASTM D5444 for sieve analysis. If the nuclear gauge is used to measure asphalt content, there is no way to recover the aggregate from the mixture for testing.
key_points: Extraction testing per ASTM D2172; nuclear gauge testing per ASTM D4125 (gauge must be calibrated); ignition method per ASTM D6307
Gradation on extracted/recovered aggregate follows ASTM D5444
Key limitation: the nuclear-gauge method does not allow aggregate recovery for further gradation testing
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and executing an asphalt-content test method during PFC plant production control.

sections.title: Mix Proportions
sections.summary: Requires adjusting PFC mix proportions whenever tolerances are exceeded, identifies faulty scales and operator weighing error as common batch-plant deficiency causes, and cross-references Figure 2-8 for other probable plant-operation causes.
sections.body: Adjust mix proportions whenever tests indicate that specified tolerances are not being met. In the case of batch plants, common causes for mixture deficiencies are faulty scales and the failure of the operator to accurately weigh the required proportions of materials. Detect failure of accurate weighing or faulty scales and take corrective measures by maintaining a close check of load weights. Figure 2-8 presents other probable causes of mixture deficiencies due to plant operations.
key_points: Adjust mix proportions when test results fall outside specified tolerances
Batch plant deficiencies commonly stem from faulty scales or operator weighing errors; monitor load weights closely to catch these before they affect the mix
Figure 2-8 (presented earlier in the chapter) catalogs additional probable causes of plant-related mixture deficiencies
sections.applicability: Applies to plant QC response when sieve/asphalt-content test results deviate from PFC job-mix-formula tolerances.

sections.title: Controlling Plant Production
sections.summary: Directs the plant inspector to sample PFC mix roughly 30 minutes into production and test promptly for gradation/asphalt content, and flags draindown risk when haul distance to the site is long.
sections.body: Normally the plant inspector obtains a sample of the PFC mix after the plant has been in production for 30 minutes. Test the sample as rapidly as possible for compliance with gradation and asphalt content requirements. If plant is too far from the construction site, draindown potentially occurs during haul due to the extended period of haul time.
key_points: Plant inspector samples PFC mix about 30 minutes into production and tests promptly for gradation/asphalt content compliance
Long haul distances risk asphalt draindown during transport to the paving site
sections.applicability: Applies to routine plant-production sampling frequency and haul-distance risk management for PFC.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Umbrella heading for PFC construction practice: rolling/pavement control, thickness sampling, storage silo limits, and temperature limits for normal-condition operations, detailed in the following subsections.
key_points: PFC construction is covered across four subsections: pavement control (2-5.4.1), pavement sampling (2-5.4.2), storage silos (2-5.4.3), and pavement operations under normal conditions (2-5.4.4)
Because PFC has no density acceptance requirement and cools rapidly, construction control instead centers on roller timing, storage-time limits, and minimum placement temperature
sections.applicability: Serves as the construction umbrella for PFC; consult the following subsections for specific rolling, sampling, storage, and temperature-limit criteria.

sections.title: Pavement Control
sections.summary: Notes PFC has no density requirement but cools rapidly, so the roller should closely follow the paver to limit drainage; rich spots in warm weather are managed by delayed rolling; seating requires two passes of a 10-metric-ton steel-wheel roller.
sections.body: A PFC pavement has no density requirements. A characteristic of this overlay is its rapid cooling. If minimum asphalt drainage is desired, ensure the roller closely follows the paver to initially set the PFC so that asphalt drainage is minimized. If drainage in the truck or the paver causes a rich spot (excess asphalt cement) in the pavement, and warm weather conditions exist (high temperatures), rolling is delayed to allow the asphalt to drain into the PFC. Two passes with a 10-metric ton (10-ton) steel-wheel roller (in static mode if a vibratory roller) is required to properly seat the PFC mix.
key_points: PFC has no density acceptance requirement, unlike dense-graded HMA
PFC cools rapidly; the roller should closely follow the paver to minimize asphalt drainage during initial set
Rich spots from truck/paver drainage in warm weather are managed by delaying rolling to let the asphalt drain into the mat
Seating compaction: two passes of a 10-metric-ton steel-wheel roller (run in static mode if the roller is vibratory-capable)
sections.applicability: Applies to rolling pattern and sequencing decisions during PFC placement under normal and warm-weather conditions.

sections.title: Pavement Sampling
sections.summary: Specifies PFC thickness sampling per ASTM D979 via coring or a minimum 100 mm square saw-cut sample, which must capture the full PFC layer thickness.
sections.body: Samples for determining thickness (ASTM D979) are taken either with a coring machine or by cutting out a sample of pavement at least 100 millimeters (4 inches) square with a concrete saw. Ensure the sample includes the entire thickness of the PFC.
key_points: Thickness sampling per ASTM D979, via coring or a minimum 100 mm (4 in.) square saw-cut sample
Samples must capture the full PFC layer thickness
sections.applicability: Applies to acceptance sampling of installed PFC thickness.

sections.title: Storage Silos
sections.summary: Limits PFC mix storage to a strict 1-hour maximum to avoid asphalt drainage and mixture segregation, favoring plant/laydown coordination to eliminate the need for extended storage altogether.
sections.body: Avoid storage of PFC mix whenever possible; the maximum allowable storage time under any circumstance is not to exceed 1 hour. Excessive storage time allows the asphalt to drain, causing segregation of the mixture. Coordination between the plant and the laydown operations eliminates the need for extended storage.
key_points: PFC mix storage should be avoided; the absolute maximum storage time is 1 hour
Extended storage causes asphalt drainage and mixture segregation
Plant/laydown coordination is the primary tool for avoiding storage delays
sections.applicability: Applies to silo/surge-bin storage-time limits for PFC mix between production and placement.

sections.title: Pavement Operations under Normal Conditions
sections.summary: Sets a 16 C (60 F) minimum existing-pavement surface temperature for PFC placement and requires rolling be completed before the mixture cools to 80 C (175 F), noting PFC cools quickly due to its thin lift and high void content.
sections.body: Guide specifications do not permit placement of PFC when the surface temperature of the existing pavement is below 16 degrees C (60 degrees F). Ensure the contractor applies the specified rolling before the mixture becomes too cool to be properly seated. Generally, perform all rolling before the PFC mixture cools to 80 degrees C (175 degrees F). A PFC cools quickly because of the thin layer of material and high void content in the thin PFC layer.
key_points: Minimum existing-pavement surface temperature for PFC placement: 16 C (60 F)
Complete all rolling before the mixture cools to 80 C (175 F)
PFC cools quickly due to its thin lift and high void content, so the rolling window is short
sections.applicability: Applies to setting minimum ambient/pavement-surface temperature limits and the rolling time window for PFC placement.

sections.title: Stone Matrix Asphalt
sections.summary: Introduces stone matrix asphalt (SMA) as an aggregate/filler/asphalt/stabilizer mixture that relies on stone-on-stone contact for rut resistance under high loads and tire pressures, with mastic filling voids and final air voids of 3-4 percent.
sections.body: SMA is a mixture of aggregate, mineral filler, asphalt cement, and a stabilizer (modified asphalt with or without the addition of cellulose or mineral fiber). SMA is designed to minimize rutting and abrasions even under high loads and high tire pressures. SMA mixtures depend on aggregate-to-aggregate contact to support traffic loads, therefore their mix design requires a higher percentage of coarse aggregate than HMA. Excess fine aggregate or too much mastic prevents the coarse aggregate particles from obtaining full contact and therefore lowers the mixture's resistance to rutting. The high void content of the mix is occupied by fine aggregate, mineral filler, asphalt cement, and a stabilizer (polymer, cellulose, or mineral fiber), which forms a mastic portion of the SMA mixture. This mastic stabilizes the coarse aggregate and reduces the final air voids in the SMA to 3 to 4 percent. SMA is comparable to HMA in regards to structural design, mix design, and construction. SMA originated in Europe and has recently been placed by state and federal agencies on projects throughout the country. The design and construction of SMA pavements are described in this chapter.
key_points: SMA = aggregate + mineral filler + asphalt cement + stabilizer (polymer and/or cellulose/mineral fiber)
Load support comes from stone-on-stone (aggregate-to-aggregate) contact, requiring a higher coarse-aggregate fraction than dense-graded HMA
Excess fines/mastic prevents full coarse-aggregate contact and reduces rutting resistance
Mastic (fines + filler + asphalt + stabilizer) fills the void structure and stabilizes coarse aggregate; final air voids target 3 to 4 percent
Structural design, mix design, and construction are comparable to HMA; SMA originated in Europe
sections.applicability: Introduces stone matrix asphalt as a rut-resistant, stone-on-stone mixture for high-load/high-tire-pressure pavements; applies broadly to the SMA design and construction guidance in 2-6.1 through 2-6.5.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Umbrella heading for the four SMA material categories: aggregates (2-6.1.1), filler (2-6.1.2), stabilizer (2-6.1.3), and asphalt (2-6.1.4), each detailed in the following subsections.
key_points: SMA materials are covered across four subsections: aggregates (2-6.1.1), filler (2-6.1.2), stabilizer (2-6.1.3), and asphalt (2-6.1.4)
SMA's mastic-based structure makes filler content and draindown-control stabilizer selection as important as the aggregate gradation itself
sections.applicability: Serves as the material-requirements umbrella for SMA mix design; consult the following subsections for specific aggregate, filler, stabilizer, and asphalt criteria.

sections.title: Aggregates
sections.summary: Sets SMA gap gradation on the No. 4 sieve with 72-80 percent coarse aggregate, 100 percent passing 19 mm, and 8-10 percent passing 75 um; cites Table 2-15 (NAPA/FHWA gradation) and Table 2-16 (coarse/fine aggregate properties), plus an ASTM C142 alternative for airfield specs.
sections.body: The gradation used for SMA is gap-graded for the coarse aggregate retained on the 4.75-millimeter (No. 4) sieve. This coarse aggregate makes up from 72 to 80 percent of the aggregate in the mix. Ensure 100 percent of the coarse aggregate passes the 19-millimeter (3/4-inch) sieve, and the amount of the fine material passing the 75-micrometer (No. 200) sieve is from 8 to 10 percent. Table 2-15 lists the gradation as recommended by the NAPA and FHWA. This gradation is based on the recommendations of a technical working group jointly representing NAPA and FHWA that reviewed the performance of SMA mixtures in place. Table 2-16 lists the recommended coarse and fine aggregate properties for SMA. Another test that is often used for airfield specs is ASTM C142, Clay Lumps and Friable Particles, which might be used in place of ASTM D3744, coarse and fine durability index.
key_points: SMA gradation is gap-graded on the No. 4 (4.75 mm) sieve; coarse aggregate is 72-80 percent of the mix, with 100 percent passing 19 mm
Material passing the 75 um (No. 200) sieve is 8-10 percent
Table 2-15 gives the NAPA/FHWA-recommended SMA gradation; Table 2-16 gives recommended coarse and fine aggregate properties
ASTM C142 (clay lumps and friable particles) may substitute for ASTM D3744 (durability index) on airfield specs
tables: Table 2-15: SMA Gradation Guideline
Table 2-16: Recommended SMA Coarse and Fine Aggregate Properties
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and specifying SMA coarse and fine aggregate gradation and quality properties.

sections.title: Filler
sections.summary: Targets 8-10 percent SMA filler passing the No. 200 sieve, higher than dense-graded HMA, with a filler-to-asphalt ratio of 1.5 or higher (versus under 1.2 for HMA); requires a well-graded filler and lists fly ash, limestone dust, and rock dust as successful materials.
sections.body: As presented in Table 2-15 for SMA mixtures, the recommended amount of aggregate filler (dust) passing the 75-micrometers (No. 200) sieve is 8 to 10 percent. This amount of filler in the SMA is higher than that usually found in dense-graded HMA. The amount of filler is important in obtaining the desired mixture air voids and in affecting the optimum asphalt content. The SMA asphalt content is sensitive to the aggregate fines and filler content. SMA mixtures commonly employ a filler-to-asphalt ratio of 1.5 and higher. In contrast, conventional dense-graded hot mix recommends a filler-to-asphalt ratio of less than 1.2. A well-graded filler with less than 20 percent of the total filler smaller than 20 micrometers (0.001 inch) is required. Commercial fillers are added by mineral filler feeder systems. Fly ash, limestone dust, and other types of rock dust have been used successfully as fillers for SMA applications.
key_points: Filler (passing 75 um / No. 200) target: 8-10 percent, higher than typical dense-graded HMA
Filler content strongly affects air voids and optimum asphalt content, since SMA asphalt content is sensitive to fines/filler
SMA filler-to-asphalt ratio is typically 1.5 or higher, versus under 1.2 for conventional dense-graded HMA
Filler gradation control: less than 20 percent of total filler finer than 20 um; added via mineral filler feeder systems
Successful filler materials include fly ash, limestone dust, and other rock dust
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting mineral filler type, gradation, and dosage for SMA mix design.

sections.title: Stabilizer
sections.summary: Explains SMA's binder-drainage tendency and the two stabilizer categories used to control it: cellulose/mineral fibers (Tables 2-13/2-14, 0.3-0.4 percent dosage) and polymer modification, noting fiber-polymer combinations outperform polymer alone at reducing draindown.
sections.body: There is a tendency for the asphalt binder to drain from the aggregate during storage, transportation, or placement because of the high asphalt content in the mix, the thick asphalt coating on the coarse aggregate, and the high voids in the aggregate skeleton. To reduce this drainage potential, stabilizers are used to stiffen the mastic or to increase the asphalt binder viscosity. These stabilizers are categorized into two groups: (1) either cellulose fibers or mineral fibers, and (2) polymers. When SMA has been placed with a combination of fibers and asphalt polymer, the fibers have been shown to perform better at reducing draindown than polymers. Tables 2-13 and 2-14 provide the requirements and test procedures to be used with cellulose and mineral fibers, respectively. The dosage rates normally used for cellulose fibers is 0.3 percent by weight of the total mix and for mineral fibers is 0.4 percent by weight of the total mix. The recommended tolerance for the fibers is 10 percent of the required fiber weight. SMA mixtures have also been placed using a polymer to modify the asphalt cement and stabilize the mixture so that fibers are not required, and there have been instances where a polymer and a fiber have been used together to stabilize SMA mixtures. Follow the manufacturer's design and construction recommendations when the standard SMA guidelines are not applicable for asphalt-polymer stabilizers.
key_points: High asphalt content, thick coarse-aggregate coating, and high skeleton voids give SMA a strong tendency toward binder drainage; stabilizers stiffen the mastic or raise binder viscosity to counter it
Two stabilizer categories: (1) cellulose or mineral fibers, (2) polymers; fiber-and-polymer combinations have outperformed polymer alone at reducing draindown
Fiber requirements: Table 2-13 (cellulose) and Table 2-14 (mineral); typical dosage 0.3 percent (cellulose) or 0.4 percent (mineral) by mix weight, plus or minus 10 percent tolerance
Polymer modified asphalt can stabilize SMA without fibers; when standard guidelines do not apply to asphalt-polymer stabilizers, follow manufacturer recommendations
tables: Table 2-13: Properties of Cellulose Fibers
Table 2-14: Properties of Mineral Fibers
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting a draindown-control stabilizer (fiber, polymer, or both) for an SMA mixture.

sections.title: Asphalt
sections.summary: Requires SMA asphalt cement per ASTM D946, D3381, or D6373 at the grade already used locally, bumped for heavy traffic under D6373, mixed at a viscosity of 170+/-20 centistokes (or per manufacturer guidance if polymer modified).
sections.body: Ensure the asphalt cement complies with the requirements of ASTM D946, ASTM D3381, or ASTM D6373, and the asphalt cement used is the grade normally used in the area by the local DOT or on previous Department of Defense (DoD) projects. When using ASTM D6373, the grade is normally bumped to be equal to that specified for heavy traffic. Ensure the temperature of the asphalt cement at the time of mixing is that required to achieve a viscosity of 170±20 centistokes. Where polymer modified asphalt cement is used, manufacturer's recommendations for mixing temperature are to be followed.
key_points: Asphalt cement per ASTM D946, D3381, or D6373, using the grade already established locally by DOT/DoD practice
Under ASTM D6373 (performance grading), the grade is typically bumped up to the heavy-traffic grade
Target mixing viscosity: 170 plus or minus 20 centistokes; polymer modified binders instead follow manufacturer mixing-temperature guidance
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting the asphalt cement grade and mixing temperature for SMA.

sections.title: Mixture Design
sections.summary: Directs SMA optimum asphalt content determination by procedures similar to section 2-4.3, with Table 2-17 (based on AASHTO MP8) giving the recommended mix design requirements (VTM, asphalt content, VMA, stability, flow, compaction, draindown).
sections.body: Determine optimum asphalt content with procedures similar to those outlined in section 2-4.3. Table 2-17 contains the recommended mix design requirements for SMA, which are based on the requirements in AASHTO MP8.
key_points: Optimum asphalt content procedure parallels the HMA method in section 2-4.3
Table 2-17 (based on AASHTO MP8) gives the SMA mix design requirements: VTM, asphalt content, VMA, stability, flow, compaction, and draindown
tables: Table 2-17: SMA Mix Design Requirements
sections.applicability: Applies to establishing the SMA job-mix-formula design targets.

sections.title: SMA Draindown Test
sections.summary: Describes the ASTM D6390 draindown test, which measures asphalt cement separating from an uncompacted SMA sample and depositing outside the wire basket, used both for mix acceptance and field-production evaluation; Table 2-17 sets the 0.3 percent (1-hour) limit.
sections.body: For the purpose of this test method (ASTM D6390), draindown is considered to be that portion of the asphalt cement that separates itself from a sample of uncompacted SMA mixture as a whole and is deposited outside the wire basket during the test. This test method is used to determine whether the amount of draindown measured for a given SMA mixture is within acceptable levels. This test method also provides an evaluation of the draindown potential of an SMA mixture produced in the field.
key_points: ASTM D6390 draindown test measures asphalt cement that separates from an uncompacted SMA sample and drips outside the wire basket
Used both to check a given mixture against acceptable draindown levels and to evaluate field-produced SMA draindown potential
Table 2-17 sets the acceptance limit at 0.3 percent maximum on a 1-hour reading
sections.applicability: Applies to laboratory and field verification of an SMA mixture's asphalt draindown potential.

sections.title: JMF Requirements
sections.summary: Lists the contractor's written job mix formula (JMF) submittal requirements for SMA: sieve-by-sieve gradation, minus-0.020-mm fines, asphalt content, stockpile blend data, stabilizer type/dosage, ingredient properties, mixing temperature, and the FHWA 0.45-power gradation chart plot, all conforming to Table 2-17.
sections.body: It is the contractor's responsibility to ensure that, in addition to meeting the aggregate gradation requirements, the produced material provides an asphalt mixture that conforms to the applicable design parameters listed in Table 2-17. Submit in writing the proposed JMF in accordance with contract specifications, including: the percentage (in units of 1 percent) of aggregate passing each specified sieve (except the 75-micrometer, No. 200, sieve) based on the total dry weight of aggregate as determined by ASTM C117 and C136; the percentage (in units of 1/10th of 1 percent) of aggregate passing the 75-micrometer (No. 200) sieve, based on the dry weight of aggregate as determined by ASTM C117; the percentage (in units of 1/10th of 1 percent) of aggregate finer than 0.020 millimeter in size, based on the dry weight of aggregate as determined by AASHTO T 88-13 (2017); the percentage (in units of 1/10th of 1 percent) of asphalt material to be added based upon the total weight of mixture; the proposed percentage of each stockpile to be used, the average gradation of each stockpile, and the proposed target value for each sieve size, with the target values and combined average stockpile gradation kept within the source document's cited gradation ranges; and the type and amount by weight of mix of stabilizer additive to be used. Additional required JMF information includes: the material sources for all ingredients; the material properties for all ingredients, including specific gravities of the individual aggregates and asphalt, the LA abrasion of the aggregates, the sand equivalent value of the combined aggregate, the flat and elongated percent of the coarse aggregate (3-to-1 and 5-to-1 ratios) retained above the 4.75 millimeter (No. 4) sieve, the plasticity index of the aggregate, the absorption of the aggregates, and the asphalt temperature/viscosity curves; the mixing temperature; the mix design test property values and curves used to develop the job mix in accordance with those provided for HMA in this chapter and also in the Asphalt Institute's MS-2; and the plot of the gradation on the FHWA 0.45 power gradation chart.
key_points: Contractor must submit a written JMF, in addition to meeting the aggregate gradation requirements, conforming to Table 2-17 design parameters

JMF submittal must report sieve-by-sieve percent passing (ASTM C117/C136), percent passing the 75 um sieve and percent finer than 0.020 mm (AASHTO T88-13) at 0.1 percent precision, and percent added asphalt at 0.1 percent precision
Stockpile blend percentages, individual stockpile gradations, and target sieve values must be reported and kept within the applicable gradation ranges

JMF must also report ingredient sources; aggregate/asphalt specific gravities; LA abrasion; sand equivalent; flat-and-elongated ratios; plasticity index; absorption; asphalt viscosity curves; mixing temperature; mix-design test values/curves; and the FHWA 0.45-power gradation chart plot
tables: Table 2-17: SMA Mix Design Requirements
sections.applicability: Applies to the contractor's written job-mix-formula (JMF) submittal package for SMA, including required gradation, ingredient, and mix-design documentation.

sections.title: Mixing Plants
sections.summary: States that SMA has been produced in both batch and drum-mix plants, but that both require adaptations to properly incorporate SMA's mastic components (filler and fiber/polymer stabilizer), detailed in the following subsections.
sections.body: SMA has been mixed in both batch and drum-mix plants. However, make required adaptations to meet the SMA components mix design.
key_points: SMA can be produced in either batch or drum-mix plants
Both plant types require adaptations to properly incorporate SMA's mastic components (filler, stabilizer/fiber)
sections.applicability: Applies to plant-type selection and adaptation planning for SMA production.

sections.title: Batch Plants
sections.summary: Describes adding mineral filler directly to the weigh hopper (with close attention to proportioning accuracy) and fiber either into the weigh hopper with the hot aggregate or, alternatively, directly into the pugmill.
sections.body: The mineral filler is added directly into the weigh hopper. Batch plants have an existing mechanism for accomplishing this; however, attention is required to assure accurate proportioning of the amounts of filler required for SMA. The fiber is also added directly into the weigh hopper, which occurs when the hot aggregate is also being placed into the hopper. An alternative method of adding the fibers directly to the pugmill as the hot aggregates are added has also been used successfully.
key_points: Mineral filler is added directly into the weigh hopper; existing batch-plant mechanisms handle this but need close attention to proportioning accuracy
Fiber is added directly to the weigh hopper concurrently with hot aggregate, or alternatively fed directly into the pugmill as hot aggregate is added
sections.applicability: Applies to batch-plant modifications for adding mineral filler and fiber stabilizer during SMA production.

sections.title: Drum-Mix Plants
sections.summary: Describes adding mineral filler and fiber directly into the drum mixer, with accurate filler proportioning required and loose fibers typically needing a separate feed system that introduces them into the aggregate stream, away from the burner flame.
sections.body: The mineral filler is added directly into the drum mixer. Attention is required to assure accurate proportioning of the amounts of filler added. The fiber is also added directly into the drum mixer. A separate feeding system is usually employed, in the case of loose fibers. Ensure these fibers are added to the aggregates to avoid direct contact with the burner flame.
key_points: Mineral filler and fiber are both added directly into the drum mixer, with close attention to filler proportioning accuracy
Loose fibers typically need a separate feed system and must be introduced into the aggregate stream, not directly into the burner flame
sections.applicability: Applies to drum-mix plant modifications for adding mineral filler and fiber stabilizer during SMA production.

sections.title: Mixing Time
sections.summary: Notes SMA mixing time exceeds dense-graded HMA: batch-plant dry-mixing time increases 5-15 seconds, and wet-mixing time increases at least 5 seconds for cellulose fiber and up to 5 seconds for mineral fiber.
sections.body: The time required to mix SMA is usually greater than that to mix dense-graded HMA. For batch plants, the dry-mixing time is increased from 5 to 15 seconds, and wet-mixing is increased at least 5 seconds for cellulose fibers and up to 5 seconds for mineral fibers.
key_points: SMA mixing time exceeds dense-graded HMA mixing time
Batch plants: dry-mixing time increases 5-15 seconds; wet-mixing time increases at least 5 seconds for cellulose fiber, up to 5 seconds for mineral fiber
sections.applicability: Applies to setting batch-plant dry- and wet-mixing cycle times for SMA.

sections.title: Storage
sections.summary: Limits SMA surge-bin storage to under 1 hour (used only to balance production) and heated/insulated storage to 4 hours unless lab testing shows no adverse binder change or excessive draindown; prohibits overnight storage.
sections.body: Temporary (less than 1 hour) storage of SMA in surge bins is used only for balanced production capacity. Limit storage in heated and insulated storage bins to 4 hours unless laboratory testing indicates that additional time is acceptable. Base acceptability on no adverse changes in binder properties and excessive draindown not occurring. Do not store mixture overnight.
key_points: Surge-bin storage (less than 1 hour) is used only to balance production capacity
Heated/insulated storage bin limit: 4 hours, extendable only if lab testing shows no adverse binder change and no excessive draindown
Overnight storage of SMA mix is prohibited
sections.applicability: Applies to setting allowable SMA storage duration in surge bins versus heated/insulated storage silos.

sections.title: Test Section
sections.summary: Requires construction of a test section to examine the contractor's SMA mixing and placement procedures, particularly important where the contractor lacks prior SMA experience.
sections.body: The construction of a test section is important to allow examination of the contractor's mixing and placement procedures. This is true if the contractor has not had experience in mixing or placing SMA.
key_points: A test section verifies the contractor's SMA mixing and placement procedures before full production
Particularly warranted when the contractor lacks prior SMA experience
sections.applicability: Applies to deciding whether to require a trial/test section before full-scale SMA production and placement.

sections.title: Placement
sections.summary: Umbrella heading for SMA placement practice: equipment selection, surface preparation, paving temperature, and compaction, detailed in the following four subsections.
key_points: SMA placement is covered across four subsections: equipment (2-6.5.1), surface preparation (2-6.5.2), paving (2-6.5.3), and compaction (2-6.5.4)
Placement control emphasizes steel-wheel rolling only, controlled mixture temperature, and careful roller-drum management given SMA's high binder content
sections.applicability: Serves as the placement umbrella for SMA; consult the following subsections for specific equipment, temperature, and compaction criteria.

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: Requires standard AC hauling/paving equipment but only steel-wheel rollers for SMA; excludes rubber-tire rollers (they pick up the rich mix) and requires care with vibratory rollers to avoid fracturing aggregate.
sections.body: The trucks, pavers, distributors, and other general equipment are the same as those used for any asphalt concrete (AC) construction. Only steel-wheel rollers are used for SMA. Rubber-tire rollers are not used since they tend to pick up the rich mix excessively. Vibratory rollers are used, but take care to prevent breakdown (fracture) of the aggregate.
key_points: General hauling/paving equipment (trucks, pavers, distributors) is the same as standard AC construction
Only steel-wheel rollers are used for SMA; rubber-tire rollers are excluded because they pick up the rich (high-asphalt) mix
Vibratory rollers may be used but must be controlled to avoid fracturing (breaking down) the coarse aggregate
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting compaction and paving equipment for SMA placement.

sections.title: Surface Preparation
sections.summary: Requires cleaning the surface of loose/deleterious material, applying a tack coat per section 3-3, and a minimum 7 C (45 F) and rising atmospheric temperature at placement.
sections.body: Clean the surface of all loose or deleterious material. Apply a tack coat as described in section 3-3. A minimum atmospheric temperature of 7 degrees C (45 degrees F) and rising is required at the time of placement.
key_points: Surface must be cleaned of loose/deleterious material before SMA placement
Tack coat is applied per section 3-3
Minimum atmospheric temperature for placement: 7 C (45 F) and rising
sections.applicability: Applies to pre-paving surface preparation and minimum ambient temperature for SMA placement.

sections.title: Paving
sections.summary: Requires SMA mixture delivery temperature high enough for good compaction without damaging the binder, capping the mixture temperature at 177 C (350 F).
sections.body: Ensure the SMA mixture, when delivered to the paver, is at a temperature sufficiently high for good compaction but not so high as to damage the asphalt binder. Never exceed 177 degrees C (350 degrees F) for the mixture temperature.
key_points: Paver-delivery temperature must be high enough for good compaction but not so high as to damage the binder
Absolute maximum SMA mixture temperature: 177 C (350 F)
sections.applicability: Applies to controlling SMA delivery and paving temperature.

sections.title: Compaction
sections.summary: Sets a 94 percent maximum-theoretical-density compaction target via nuclear gauge control, steel-wheel and careful vibratory rolling only, moistened roller drums to prevent binder adhesion, and a 60 C (140 F) minimum before opening to traffic.
sections.body: Compact the SMA to a minimum of 94 percent of maximum theoretical density. Use steel-wheel rollers for rolling. Vibratory rollers are used provided that the aggregate is not excessively crushed. Rubber-tire rollers do not perform well with SMA due to the high amounts of asphalt cement in the mixture causing asphalt buildup on the wheels. Continue rolling until the required density is obtained. This is usually controlled through the use of a nuclear density gauge. Due to the amount of binder coating the aggregate particles, it is important that the roller drums be properly moistened with water containing small amounts of detergent to prevent adhesion. Ensure traffic remains off the SMA surface until it has cooled below a minimum of 60 degrees C (140 degrees F). One method that has been used to increase the rate of cooling to allow for earlier trafficking is flooding with water from a truck after the completion of all rolling.
key_points: Minimum compacted density: 94 percent of maximum theoretical density, controlled via nuclear density gauge

Steel-wheel rollers are standard; vibratory rollers are acceptable if aggregate crushing is avoided; rubber-tire rollers are unsuitable because of asphalt buildup on the wheels from SMA's high binder content
Roller drums must be kept moist (water plus a small amount of detergent) to prevent binder adhesion/pickup
Traffic is excluded until the SMA surface cools below 60 C (140 F); water flooding after rolling can accelerate cooling to allow earlier trafficking
sections.applicability: Applies to SMA compaction density targets, roller selection, and post-rolling cooling/trafficking control.

sections.title: Warm-Mix Asphalt
sections.summary: Covers warm-mix asphalt (WMA), produced/placed at 110-132 C (230-270 F) via viscosity-modifying additives or foaming, generally meeting HMA requirements; primary benefit is reduced production emissions plus improved cool-weather workability, with mix moisture needing monitoring.
sections.body: In recent years, processes that allow mixtures to be constructed at lower temperatures have been developed, and these lower temperature mixtures are referred to as warm-mix asphalt. A number of processes have been used, but specific processes are not discussed here. These processes allow the asphalt mixture to be mixed and placed at temperatures of 132 degrees C (270 degrees F) down to 110 degrees C (230 degrees F). The techniques involve using additives to change the viscosity of the asphalt at the higher temperatures or a foaming process. Generally, these warm mixes meet the requirements for HMA. While there has been little use on airfields, there has been significant use on highways. It is anticipated that use of warm-mix asphalt (WMA) increases significantly on airfields in future years. Early performance of WMA has been good. Use UFGS 32 12 15.13 as the guide specification for WMA. Prior to using WMA, contact the Pavements Discipline Working Group (DWG) or their designated representative. The primary purpose of WMA is to reduce emissions during production. The additional cost for producing WMA is often offset by the savings in fuel cost. Hence, WMA potentially is a little lower cost than HMA or it might be a little higher depending on location and other factors. Besides reducing emissions, WMA also has other benefits including improved workability and ability to provide a mixture easier to compact during cooler weather. There have been a number of studies for roads and for airfields comparing the performance of WMA and HMA. So far, studies have shown that WMA and HMA have similar performance characteristics. One thing that has to be monitored, when WMA is used just as with HMA, is the moisture in the mix. Since mix temperatures are lower with WMA, the amount of moisture tends to be a little higher as specified in the mix design. So far, this has not been a significant problem but it is one that has to be monitored. There are approximately 30 products/techniques for producing WMA. All of these have not been determined to be viable for airfields. UFGS 32 12 15.16 provides an approach for determining viable products. There are no significant differences in production, placement, and compaction of WMA and HMA.
key_points: WMA is produced/placed at reduced temperatures, 110-132 C (230-270 F), versus conventional HMA, using viscosity-modifying additives or a foaming process; generally still meets HMA requirements
Limited airfield use to date but significant highway use; airfield use is expected to grow, and early WMA performance has been good
Guide specification: UFGS 32 12 15.13; contact the Pavements Discipline Working Group (DWG) before using WMA

Primary benefit is reduced production emissions; cost may run slightly lower or higher than HMA depending on fuel savings versus additive cost; also improves workability/compactability in cool weather
Studies show WMA and HMA have similar performance; mix moisture tends to run slightly higher at WMA's lower production temperatures and must be monitored

About 30 WMA products/techniques exist; not all are airfield-viable; UFGS 32 12 15.16 provides an approach for determining viable products; production, placement, and compaction otherwise do not differ significantly from HMA
sections.applicability: Applies to evaluating and specifying warm-mix asphalt as a lower-temperature alternative or supplement to conventional HMA production, particularly where emissions reduction or cool-weather workability is a driver.
